I must cast, Most Eminent Prince—I might almost say against my will—the die of my reputation; for I am now committing these first fruits of the Coptic, or Egyptian, language to the judgment of the mind and eyes under the splendor of your Most Eminent Name, prepared to await the fair and unfair judgments of various men with a steady spirit. And indeed, these works would have remained hidden along with their author, just like all the other materials I have already prepared regarding the ancient and hitherto unknown symbolic wisdom of the Egyptians through unwearied study and persistent effort, had not the dutiful persistence of friends, armed entreaties, and a certain friendly force extorted them from my hands with almost daily demands. # Letter of Dedication

...beyond doubt, I would have strengthened [my mind], and content with private delight, I would have adopted that saying of Antigenidas: *I sing for myself and for the Muses.* <note>Antigenidas was a famous Theban flute player who reportedly told a talented but ignored pupil to "play for me and the Muses."</note> For as to what some people kept reminding me—that I ought to leave some trace behind to testify to posterity that I had lived, so that I might not "wholly die" and that a "great part of me" might avoid Libitina <note>Kircher is quoting the Roman poet Horace; Libitina was the goddess of funerals, here representing death and oblivion.</note>—this did not move me in the least, for the mere immortality of a name has always seemed to me a far too meager reward for such great labors. I also remembered that famous and wise pronouncement by Severinus Boethius <note>A 6th-century philosopher whose *Consolation of Philosophy* was a standard text in Renaissance education.</note>:

> ->*But if you think that your life is prolonged*<-
> ->*By the mortal breath of a Name,*<-
> ->*When the late day snatches this also from you,*<-
> ->*A second death already awaits you.*<-
> <note>original: *Quod si putatis longius vitam trahi / Mortalis aura Numinis / Cum sera vobis rapiet hoc etiam dies / Iam vos secunda mors manet.*</note>

Furthermore, if one must set sail for glory and the memory of posterity, the Royal Prophet <note>King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> opens a different sea for religious men: namely, that through constant exercise of solid virtues and contempt for superficial goods, they should pursue an immortality of name that will never perish. For I had learned long ago from his divine prophecy that "the just man will be in eternal memory." <note>A reference to Psalm 112:6.</note> Therefore, the arguments of those who contended that "no one is born for himself alone" <note>A famous Stoic principle cited by Cicero.</note> seemed to carry somewhat more weight; and consequently, whatever talents one has received, entrusted to him by God the Best and Greatest... <note>The sentence continues on the next page.</note>

# Letter of Dedication

## Letter of Dedication.

...[be remembered forever, so that it] might not be unworthy of the public light in the judgment of others, and by no means to be begrudged to the public. But I had not a few things to oppose to these arguments; and first indeed, being conscious of my own insignificance, I considered the kindness of friends toward me to be a judge not entirely impartial. Moreover, this was constantly present in my mind: who will read these things? Or if they can read them, who will apply their mind to understand languages so foreign and so far removed from our world? For I was not ignorant of the sharp wits of the **Critics** of this age, and that this century abounds in its own <term>Aristarches</term> <note>Aristarchus of Samothrace was a famous ancient scholar known for his rigorous criticism; Kircher uses the name here to describe the harsh, pedantic critics of his own time.</note>. For if I follow closely in the footsteps of those who have written on the most difficult matters, they will soon "cut the throat" of my "barbarous style" with their severe <term>obelisks</term> <note>In early textual scholarship, an "obelisk" (†) was a mark placed next to text deemed suspicious or incorrect. Kircher is using a metaphor for his work being harshly edited or rejected.</note>; but if I wander somewhat more freely into the fields of <term>philology</term> <note>The study of language and literature. At this time, it often involved the decipherment of ancient or exotic scripts.</note>, they will repeatedly say that I do an injury to weightier matters by laying on a veneer of wordy **bombast** <note>original: *ampullis*, literally "flasks," used by Roman poets to describe puffed-up, pretentious speech.</note>. For these reasons, I argued with my friends that I should do nothing. Yet I did not, for that reason, pursue the allurements of words, veneers, and <term>curling-irons</term> <note>original: *calamistra*; Kircher uses this metaphorically to describe an overly artificial or decorative rhetorical style.</note> in a grave and difficult subject; let those who are entirely devoid of substance hang this <term>ivy</term> <note>A reference to the proverb "Good wine needs no bush [ivy]"; taverns would hang ivy to signal wine for sale, so Kircher means decorative flourishes are only needed to mask a lack of content.</note> on their writings. To me, the investigation of difficult and hidden things seems to shine more purely in its own native dress.

Therefore, more than all these things, [I considered] the honor of God, in whom...

# Letter of Dedication.

[...I] was aiming at only one thing: care for the public good. This conviction is what caused me—a man who has never highly valued the fickle breath of popular favor—to be unable to avoid the waves of slander by remaining in hiding. While it would have been no trouble at all to appear wise by keeping silent, I have now thrown myself into that arena where, to speak with the **Comic poet** <note>original: *Comico*; Kircher likely refers to the Roman playwright Plautus, who often used metaphors of the wrestling school or arena.</note>, one's reputation is often **worn down** <note>original: *defudasci-tur*, a term suggesting physical exhaustion or being spent, used here metaphorically for the struggle of public intellectual life.</note> at great cost.

But in this uncertain struggle of the mind, the singular protection of your **Most Eminent Name** <note>A reference to Cardinal Francesco Barberini (1597–1679), Kircher's powerful patron and the nephew of Pope Urban VIII.</note> restores and revives me. I have been led by many reasons to mark the front of this work with its extraordinary splendor. 

First of all, because Your Eminence commanded me to undertake this task; encouraged me to dare it; supplied the necessary means so that I might be able to achieve it; and your own immense care and incredible zeal in investigating **hidden literature** <note>original: *reconditis literaturis*; this refers to the study of ancient, obscure, or "lost" languages like Coptic and Egyptian hieroglyphs, which were Kircher's primary focus.</note> acted as a spur for me to proceed more fervently. Finally, so that I might act cautiously and considerately, your own sharpest judgment moved me during the review of these matters, as did your other virtues. I would rather praise the greatness of these virtues through silence than—as <term>Suetonius</term> <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus (c. 69–122 AD), a Roman historian famous for his biographies of the Caesars.</note> once said of <term>Augustus</term> <note>The first Roman Emperor, famously portrayed by Suetonius; Kircher is comparing his patron to Augustus to emphasize his status as a grand protector of the arts and sciences.</note>—to touch upon them "sparingly and meagerly." 

To all these things is finally added your singular affection for our **Society** <note>The Society of Jesus, or the Jesuits, the religious order to which Kircher belonged.</note>. Although I doubt I can respond to this affection as an equal, it must still be counted as part of my gratitude that I am at least striving not to be ungrateful.

<summary>Kircher explains that his dedication to the public good and the direct command and support of Cardinal Francesco Barberini overcame his fear of critics. He praises the Cardinal's intellectual zeal and compares his patronage to that of the Emperor Augustus.</summary>

## *Dedication Letter.*

Moved by these reasons, behold this **Coptic** or **Egyptian Forerunner** <note>original: *Prodromus Coptus*; Kircher uses the word "Prodromus" (Forerunner) to indicate this work is an introductory precursor to his larger, more ambitious planned works on Egypt.</note>, which, at last, after the long dangers of a difficult journey and various labors, now presents itself whole and unharmed to your **Most Eminent** gaze—a faithful messenger of things as new as they are rare and most deeply hidden. It will be your part to receive it with that same openness with which you usually welcome the debut of new discoveries. For even if its language is somewhat simple, and at first glance seems unpolished and rough, I believe you will nonetheless be pleased by its wonderful variety of expression and—the heart of the matter—the manifold revelation of unknown things. I have sent it ahead for no other purpose than to reveal what I am preparing in my forthcoming works concerning the **sacred sculptures of the Egyptians** <note>original: *sacris AEgyptiorum sculpturis*; this is Kircher's term for hieroglyphs, which he viewed as mystical symbols encoding divine secrets rather than a phonetic alphabet.</note>, and to demonstrate openly how much light a vast knowledge of foreign languages can shed upon more secret studies and disciplines.

However, if this work does not quite meet your expectations, I ask that you excuse it as a work born only from the late-night labors of my spare hours. Yet you may rest assured that my other work—which will be as much more excellent than this as **Philosophy** is rightly judged higher and more sublime than **Grammar**—will easily make up for any shortcomings here. I speak, I say, of the **revived Oedipus of Hieroglyphic enigmas** <note>original: *Hieroglyphicorum... redivivum Oedipum*; a reference to Kircher's future masterpiece, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*. In Greek mythology, Oedipus solved the riddle of the Sphinx; Kircher styles himself as a "new Oedipus" who will finally crack the code of the Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>. This

## *Dedication Letter.*

For I confess it is small, and nothing but a certain rudimentary start, or, as it were, a first sketch. However it may be, I trust it will receive splendor from your **purple** <note>original: *purpura*; this refers to the Cardinal’s rank and the distinctive color of his robes, suggesting that his patronage ennobles the humble book.</note>, and (if I may be permitted to say so) that you may receive some from it, so that this love or honor of yours for the finest arts may surely spread to foreigners and to posterity. May it spread, I say, to your praise and as an example for others. When I find this has been achieved, I will consider that I have obtained no small fruit from my labor. May God keep your **Eminence** safe for as long as possible, as the glory and ornament of the Catholic Church. Farewell.

**W**hen once, Most Eminent Prince, a sudden rumor spread among the Corinthians that Philip of Macedon was threatening the city with a vast army, and the citizens were diligently preparing whatever might be of use to endure a siege: that **day-liver** <term>hemerobios</term> <note>original: *ἡμερόβιος*; a Greek term for one who lives from day to day, specifically referring here to the minimalist lifestyle of the Cynic philosopher Diogenes.</note> Diogenes is said to have laid aside his philosopher's cap and cloak—filthy and covered in squalor—and for several days rolled that famous tub of his **up and down** <term>ano te kai kato</term> <note>original: *ἄνώ τε καὶ κάτω*; a Greek idiom meaning "back and forth" or "to and fro."</note> over a hill near the city, as if he were about to undertake some great task.

## Preface.

...with a certain new and previously unheard-of kind of labor, he wished to roll, re-roll, roll under, and roll down his tub. Since many wondered at this, being astonished by such an unusual sight, they asked what he intended by this unaccustomed rolling of his vessel. He replied: "Lest, while everyone else is busy, I alone should seem idle."

You will understand, if I am not mistaken, Great Prince, what I intend by this "prelude" to my <term>Prodromus</term> <note>The title *Prodromus Coptus* translates as "The Coptic Precursor." This work was designed as a preliminary study to pave the way for his later, more massive volumes on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>. When I was summoned to the City <note>Rome, which Kircher describes as the center of the intellectual world.</note> by your singular favor, I saw the most learned men in this "theater of the world" striving to serve the cause of letters and posterity through reading, writing, teaching, and other competitive efforts. I saw them fighting with "Palladian engines" <note>A metaphor for tools of wisdom, named after Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom. Kircher views scholarship as a form of holy siege warfare against darkness.</note> against <term>ignorance</term> <note>original Greek: *ἀγνοίαν* (agnoian).</note> with successful warfare; for that purpose, they repeatedly drew up new battle lines to rush upon ignorance and its allies with both edge and point <note>A fencing metaphor (*caesim et punctim*) meaning to attack with both the side and the tip of the blade—essentially, a total assault.</note> under the most excellent leaders.

Mindful of that saying of Diogenes—certainly worthy of such a philosopher—it seemed right for me, according to my meager ability, to come forward into their midst, lest among so many distinguished soldiers of proven virtue, I should be the only idler among the crowd. If I remained still, I would have to acknowledge that the saying of Hesiod 
<margin>
Hesiod, 
*Theogony*.
</margin>
rightly applied to me: that I was a <term>useless burden on the earth</term> <note>original Greek: *ἐτώσιον ἄχθος ἀρούρης* (etosian achthos aroures). This was a common classical insult for someone who consumes resources without contributing to society.</note>. However, while I was searching for a suitable place to roll this "philosophical tub" in this skirmish and truly Apolline expedition <note>An expedition dedicated to Apollo, the god of light, music, and truth.</note>, and while I was diligently looking around at the great variety of occupations and studies on which I saw each person already intent,

### Preface.

<margin>The difficulty of the subject matter.</margin>
...matter, considering in which part of this literary field I might most effectively apply my efforts. Behold! With every other post already occupied, I saw that only those most ancient ruins of the **Egyptians** remained for me: the crumbling walls of monuments half-buried by the injury of time. For, besides that difficult investigation of Egyptian antiquities and sacred mysteries lying hidden under <term>hieroglyphic</term> <note>Kircher believed hieroglyphs were symbols of deep, occult wisdom rather than a phonetic writing system.</note> disciplines—which no one until now (as far as I can know) has attempted—the restoration of the ancient Egyptian language, which we call **Coptic**, was also entrusted to me. This task has provided a store of labor all the greater because the subject matter is both rarer and more difficult than others.

This is especially true since, amidst the great inconstancy and change of human affairs, nothing is more difficult or more arduous than to write a narrative of things which the antiquity of time has gradually removed far from human memory and so hidden that they seem to escape all light of the intellect. In such a task, the unexplored antiquity of the subject matter offers a very dark ambiguity to those writing; and for those reading, it sometimes undermines their belief, because the description of the ages is abstruse, entangled in the infinite controversies of disagreeing **authors**, and extremely complex. Have I not, therefore, taken upon myself a field so rugged and blocked by countless difficulties, especially without a guide who knows the paths...

## Preface.

<margin>Much darkness, much error.</margin>
...to a man entering, that well-known saying of the Hebrews will appropriately apply: **"Increasing darkness increases wandering"** <note>original Hebrew: *Marbeh choshek marbeh to'ah*</note>? For where there is a great mist of darkness and an unknown path, many errors and falls, and frequent stumbles, must necessarily occur. Therefore, I am not unaware that I am embarking on a task full of dangerous risk <note>original: *aleæ*, literally "a game of dice," implying a high-stakes gamble</note>; while I strive to establish something certain not about some common or familiar language, but about the most ancient language of the Egyptian Sages. To this day, it remains as unknown to Europeans as its ancient origins are still undiscovered even among the Egyptians themselves, having been corrupted over succeeding centuries by the mingling of many different nations. But because there is no darkness so great that at least some ray of light does not shine through it, nor are there intellectual knots so tight that the keen diligence of a human mind—burning with the love of truth—cannot untie them; I certainly believed I would perform a service that would be in no way unwelcome, not only to those who study the more hidden depths of antiquity but to the entire Republic of Letters <term>Republic of Letters</term> <note>The 'Respublica Literaria' was the international community of scholars and intellectuals in the 17th century who shared knowledge through correspondence.</note>. I felt this would be the case if, just as I have done with other Egyptian monuments that have lain hidden until now, I were to apply my modest efforts to restoring their language or idiom. This is a work undertaken not so much by the impulse of my own mind (otherwise ready for any difficulties), as by the encouragement of most learned men, among whom a truly preeminent place is deservedly held by the Most Distinguished Lord, Nicolas-Claude Fabri— <note>The text cuts off mid-name; it refers to Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc (1580–1637), a famous French astronomer and patron of science who encouraged Kircher's Coptic studies.</note>

# CHAPTER I.
## Concerning the Etymology of the word "Coptos".

Just as many other records of the learned demonstrate, writers have often entangled themselves in great errors through ignorant explanations of etymologies and foreign words that were poorly understood; this is shown by those who have pulled the word **Koptos** <note>original: *κόπτος* (Greek script)</note> in different directions of meaning.

<margin>Koptos is not derived from the word Egypt.</margin>
And indeed, those who want this name, **Koptos**, to be the same as the word **Egypt** <note>original: *Aegyptus*</note>—relying on truly weak conjectures—show how little progress they have made in the knowledge of the Arabic and Coptic languages, as we shall see later.

<margin>Nor from the first King of Egypt whom they call Chibt.</margin>
<margin>Leo Africanus, Book 8.</margin>
Others, however, want to trace its **etymology** <term>Etymology</term> <note>The study of the origin and history of words.</note> from that King who first bestowed the name of "Egypt" upon the land anciently called **Mitsraim** <note>The Hebrew name for Egypt, referring to the son of Ham in the Bible.</note>, **Aeria**, or **Oceania** <note>*Aeria* (misty/airy) and *Oceania* are ancient poetic or mythical names used by classical authors for the land of Egypt.</note>; according to Leo Africanus <note>Joannes Leo Africanus (c. 1494–1554), a diplomat and author of the famous *Description of Africa*.</note>, the Egyptians call this king **Chibth** in their common tongue. But these writers wander further from the truth, as there is a significant difference to be considered between "Copts" and "Chibth."

<margin>Koptos is derived from the city of Coptos.</margin>
Finally, there are others who derive the origin of this whole word from the city of **Coptos** <note>An ancient city in Upper Egypt, modern-day Qift, which was a major trading hub.</note>; these, if I may say so, seem to **speak Coptic** <note>original: *κοπτίζειν* (koptizein). Nevertheless, since plausible reasons arise for each of the opinions just reviewed, it seemed appropriate to bring them here for examination; so that by their reasons and arguments first...

## Chapter I. Concerning the Etymology of Coptos.

Therefore, those first people who are accustomed to commonly confusing **Gyptas** <note>original: *γύπτας* (Greek)</note> with the word **Egypt** <note>original: *Aegyptus*</note> bring forward no other reason for their opinion except for a mere similarity. This is a similarity which the Arabic word **Kopti** <note>original: *قبطي*</note> and the Coptic word **Gyptias** or **Geptias** <note>original: *γύπτιας* or *γέπτιας*</note> possess in both sound and meaning relative to the word **Egypt**. But anyone can see that these people rely on a weak foundation. For if the aforementioned words are examined a bit more carefully, they will be found to be related and **homophonous** <term>Homophonous</term> <note>Words that sound similar but have different meanings or origins.</note>—sounding alike—but not **homonymous** <term>Homonymous</term> <note>Sharing the same name or linguistic root.</note>.

<margin>
The Copts call Egypt by its proper name, *Chemi*, and the Arabs call it *Mesra*.
</margin>

For I believe it is well known to those who have even slightly tasted <note>The author uses the Latin idiom *extremis labris*, "with the edge of the lips," to describe a beginner's or superficial knowledge.</note> the elements of the said languages, that this word **Gyptias** in this context does not properly mean "Egypt" in either the Coptic language or the Arabic word **Kopti**. Since the Copts properly denote Egypt by the word **Chemi** <note>original: *χήμι*</note>, just as the Arabs signify the same through the word **Mesra** <note>original: *مصر* (Misr)</note>, these things are clearly evident from our Coptic-Arabic **Onomasticon** <term>Onomasticon</term> <note>A dictionary or vocabulary of proper names; the author is likely referring to a specific manuscript he is studying.</note>. Thus the title...

## Chapter I. On the Etymology of Coptos

...they began to call Egypt by the name *Chibth* <note>The Arabic word for Egypt, *Qibt*, from which we get the word Copt.</note>. Having been instructed by their neighboring Copts, the Ethiopians call Egypt by no other name than **ምድረ ፡ ገብጽ** <note>original: *Midre Gebts*</note>, that is, the "land of Egypt."

Since this is the case, those authors judge most correctly who derive this etymology from Coptos, once a most famous city of Egypt and the capital of the Thebaid <note>A region of ancient Egypt named after the city of Thebes.</note>. # CHAPTER II.
## On the customs and institutions of the Coptites.

**C**onsidering that the location, fame, etymology, and other matters pertaining to the city of Coptos were examined in the preceding chapter, nothing now remains except that we also briefly declare what kind of people those Coptites were—from whom the Coptic language derived its name—and what their way of life was; lest we seem to have omitted anything worthy of consideration in this matter.

<margin>What was the religion of the Coptites before the coming of Christ?</margin>
It must be noted, therefore, that throughout all that time preceding the coming of human salvation <note>This refers to the era before the birth of Jesus Christ.</note>, the inhabitants of the city of Coptos were imbued with no other religion than that which was common to all of Egypt,

<margin>The worship of beasts.</margin>
namely, the worship of the Sun, the Moon, and of irrational animals—I mean dogs, cats, crocodiles, and other similar creatures. They were so deeply immersed in this worship that the Satiric poet <note>The author refers here to the Roman poet Juvenal.</note> seems, not without reason, to rail against them;

<margin>Juvenal, Satire 15.</margin>
> *Who does not know, Bithynian Volusius, what monsters*
> *mad Egypt worships?* <note>original Latin: *Quis nescit Volusi Bithynice qualia demens Ægyptus portenta colat?*</note> *and a little later*
> *Whole towns venerate the Dog, but no one worships Diana.* <note>original Latin: *Oppida tota Canem venerantur, nemo Dianam.* In this context, Juvenal is mocking the Egyptians for worshiping the dog-headed Anubis while neglecting the traditional Roman gods of the hunt like Diana.</note>

But when, in the course of time, as the Sun of Justice <term>Sun of Justice: A common metaphorical title for Jesus Christ, derived from the Book of Malachi</term> rose upon the world, Egypt was led through the Holy Apostles and their successors to the true faith of Christ...

<margin>
The love of religion among the Coptites converted to Christ.
</margin>
...the faith was brought and the seeds of the Christian religion were sown everywhere; they grew into a fruitful harvest most especially in Egypt, being so close to the source of the new Gospel. Many Egyptians, driven by a love for evangelical perfection, withdrew to those places which, being far removed from the noise of vain worldly affairs, were most suited for the contemplation of heavenly things. Palladius <note>Palladius of Galatia (c. 363–420 AD) was a bishop and chronicler of early Christian monasticism.</note> writes in his *Lausiac History* 
<margin>
Palladius in the *Lausiac History*. <note>The *Historia Lausiaca* is a primary source on the lives of the Desert Fathers.</note>
</margin>
that the desert of the Thebaid <note>The Thebaid was a region in ancient Upper Egypt, named after its capital, Thebes, which became a famous center for early Christian hermits and monks.</note> was such a place. Since the city of Coptos was very near to this desert, the followers of the monastic life chose it as their home. They were drawn partly by the convenience of obtaining the things they needed for survival (as it was adjacent to the wilderness), from which circumstance they were later called "Coptites." They also chose it so that this place—where they saw so many monuments of ancient superstition and which was once infested by the furies of demons—might be transformed into a dwelling place for the Holy Spirit, initiated through the pious studies of the monks and the holy disciplines of the Christian life.

<margin>
The Coptites were the first to rescue the ancient Egyptian language from destruction, and they were the first to call it "Coptic" after the city of Coptos.
</margin>
And these are the people who rescued that ancient Egyptian language from total destruction—even if, as usually happens with the changing of kingdoms, it had become quite corrupted. This destruction was not far off as the empire of Muhammad <note>Original Latin: *Mahumetis*. This refers to the expansion of the Islamic Caliphate in the 7th century and the subsequent linguistic shift from Egyptian/Coptic to Arabic.</note> grew. They illustrated the language with various writings and ensured it was propagated down to our own times. It was named after the town of Coptos because, while the language died out in the rest of Egypt as other languages were introduced, it was preserved solely by the Coptite inhabitants of that city.

The second was that he should forbid the art of the **transmutation of metals**; <note>Diocletian famously ordered the burning of ancient books on alchemy (the transmutation of base metals into gold) to prevent the Egyptians from funding future revolts.</note> for he feared lest the Egyptians, having become wealthier from it and having gathered an army, might perhaps cause much trouble for the Romans in the future. <margin>The institution of the Year of Diocletian.</margin>
He allowed the entire ancient Egyptian year 1031—of which the last day was June 12th—to proceed from the era of Nabonassar <note>original: "à Nabonassaro." The Era of Nabonassar was a chronological era beginning in 747 BC, used by ancient astronomers like Ptolemy to track celestial events.</note>. And assuming 311 years <note>The number of years since Egypt came under Roman rule under Augustus.</note>, on account of the 77 cycles <note>Referencing the 4-year leap year cycle.</note> elapsed since the first year of the Empire of **Octavian Caesar Augustus**, in which all past leap years <term>bissextiles: years containing an extra "intercalary" day to keep the calendar aligned with the sun</term> were included, he ordered that on the 13th day of that month, just as many days should also be counted as intercalary <term>intercalary: days inserted into a calendar to make it follow the seasons</term>. 

Then the 78th day of the current year 312 would fall on the day following the new moon of Virgo (which was on the 28th day), namely on the sixth day of the week <note>original: "feriam scilicet sextam." In the ecclesiastical calendar, the sixth feria is Friday.</note>, **August 29th**, and this day would always thereafter be the very beginning of the month of **Thoth** <note>The first month of the Egyptian and Coptic calendar.</note> of that new reformed year. And just as after the last month those 5 days were always intercalated: this would not happen except in the first 3 common Julian years, and in the fourth leap year, another likewise...

The Coptic Era <note>original: "tarich alkubti"</note>, which descendants later began to call the **Era of the Martyrs** <note>original: "tarich al-fchahada"</note>, remains in use to this day. Ignatius, the Patriarch of Antioch <note>Ignatius Ni'matallah, who served as the Syriac Orthodox Patriarch of Antioch from 1557 to 1576 and collaborated with Western scholars on calendar reform.</note>, mentions this persecution and the Era of Martyrs. When he was consulted about these matters by **Scaliger** <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a leading scholar of the Renaissance known for his revolutionary work in chronology and history.</note>, he responded to the inquiries in a certain Arabic letter as follows:

> And also, you have asked about the **History of the Martyrs** used by the **Copts**, what it is and what the reason is for naming it by this name. Know that it begins from the nineteenth year of the Great King **Diocletian**, in which persecution against **Christianity** <note>original: "al-nazareth," literally "the Nazarenes," a common term for Christians in Arabic.</note> increased; he ordered the destruction of their churches and the killing of everyone who would not sacrifice to their idols. By this command, there were martyred at his hand, from the believers and the Coptic people, **one hundred and forty-four thousand, seven hundred souls**. From this day, the Coptic Era begins, and it is called the **Era of the Martyrs**, meaning those whose blood was shed by Diocletian.

<note>The following text is a phonetic transliteration of the Arabic passage above, provided in the original manuscript for scholars to read the Arabic sounds in Latin script.</note>

## Chapter II. On Coptic Customs.

I was very much in doubt regarding the system of the Coptic Era <term>Coptic Era: Also known as the Era of the Martyrs (*Anno Martyrum*), it dates from the beginning of the reign of Diocletian in 284 AD, whose persecutions were particularly severe in Egypt</term>, inasmuch as it seemed suspicious to me, not without reason, when I treated it previously; but I finally discovered it to be true, not only in other Arabic authors, but also in this Manuscript, with the Copts <term>Copt: An Egyptian Christian</term> themselves confirming it. For throughout their books, having indicated the name and profession of the Author, they immediately subjoin the number of years elapsed since the passing of their Martyrs <note>original: *à Martyrum suorum transitu*</note>. Since I have finished discussing what I thought should be said about the Martyrs, let us now proceed to other matters.

Furthermore, among the various rites of the Eastern Churches, the Coptic (or Egyptian) practices in the administration of sacred things are shown to be most closely aligned with Ethiopian rites. This is abundantly demonstrated not only by the *Rituals* (as they are commonly called) but also by the *Liturgies* <term>Liturgy: The prescribed form of public worship, particularly the Eucharist</term> shared by both nations. Which I translate from the Coptic as: *I believe, I believe, I believe and I confess until the final breath of my soul, that this very thing (which is in my hand) is that living body of Your Only-begotten Son, our Lord, our God, and our Savior Jesus Christ, etc.* These words correspond entirely to the Ethiopian version, as we shall see later. Indeed, I find no other cause for this affinity than that the Egyptian and Ethiopian Church, just as it was always administered by a single Bishop—specifically the Patriarch of Alexandria—so it was imbued by him with almost the same rites and ceremonies, and easily neglected others. ## Chapter II. On Coptic Customs.

<margin>Just as the religion of the Egyptians and Ethiopians was once common, so also after Christ.</margin>
...and the [Ethiopian] profane Church and idolatrous religion, which Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a 1st-century BC Greek historian who wrote about Egyptian and Ethiopian history.</note> teaches was common to both nations. For daily experience teaches us that rites, ceremonies, and customs follow the Church and its head.

<margin>Why the Ethiopians call their era the "Era of the Martyrs."</margin>
<margin>Why the Ethiopian era is called "of grace."</margin>
And from what has been said, it is also clear why the Ethiopians use the same "Era of the Martyrs" as the Copts. For since they constituted one Church under one Pastor, and during the dreadful persecution of Diocletian <note>Roman Emperor Diocletian (reigned 284–305 AD), whose reign marked the final, most severe persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire; the Coptic calendar begins with his ascension to the throne in 284 AD.</note>, not only the Egyptians but also the Ethiopians were harassed and carried away by the most grievous torments for the name of Christ, obtaining the crown of martyrdom; it was fitting that they should enjoy a common era—namely an <term>epoch</term> <note>A fixed starting point in time used to calculate a chronological era.</note>, or root—from which they would take the beginning of the years to be counted, in memory of the grace of martyrdom granted by God to so many saints. Hence,

<margin>Scaliger, Book 7, *On the Correction of Time*, in the Ethiopian annotations, folio 339, Paris edition.</margin>
<margin>What the "Year of Grace" is among the Ethiopians.</margin>
I wonder that Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a leading scholar of the Renaissance who specialized in historical chronology.</note>, who is otherwise so perceptive, was so ready to admit his ignorance in the evaluation of these "Years of Grace"; his words are:
> *The Ethiopians call the Era of Diocletian, which they use, the Year of Grace; I do not know the reason for this name.*

And at the end of his discourse: *I struggled quite a bit before I was able to understand these years of grace.* But it is no wonder that the man erred in this, as in many other things, as one who has either not seen their books or, having seen them, did not understand them.

Furthermore, just as the Copt-Ethiopian Church in its early times [was established] with holy customs and institutions...

<margin>
The Schism of the Coptic and Ethiopian Church.
</margin>
...once instructed, it made excellent progress in Christian perfection. Yet, as time passed (such is the changeability and inconstancy of human affairs), it was torn away from the universal body of the Church at various times by one schism after another. Infected by the wicked dogmas of Dioscorus <note>Dioscorus was the Patriarch of Alexandria from 444 to 451 AD; he was deposed at the Council of Chalcedon, leading to the lasting split between the Oriental Orthodox and the Roman/Byzantine Churches.</note> and others, it ceased to be holy. Nothing remained to it except the rites and ceremonies used in performing sacred duties, which it always kept intact despite the schism. This is evident from their records, which are preserved here in Rome to this day. In these records—at least as far as I have been able to observe—although specific heresies and other notable errors are not found, manifest signs of the schisms that occurred at various times appear everywhere. For they recognize no other head of the Church besides the Alexandrian Pontiff, or Patriarch.

<margin>
The Copto-Ethiopian Church recognizes no one besides the Alexandrian Pontiff.
</margin>
In their liturgies as well, I find many things added that are missing from the ancient liturgies of the Fathers—Cyril, Basil, and Gregory <note>The Coptic Church primarily uses three Eucharistic liturgies named after St. Basil the Great, St. Gregory the Theologian, and St. Cyril of Alexandria.</note>. **H**aving reviewed those matters which occurred to be said concerning the ecclesiastical rites and ceremonies used by the Copt-Ethiopian Church; a not insignificant doubt now arises, namely whether the aforementioned Church used any language other than those already mentioned in its sacred services, or not. <margin>Whether colonies were sent from Syria into Egypt and Ethiopia.</margin>

->## Chapter III. On the Coptic-Ethiopian Colonies.<-

And this is the explanation of the inscription carved upon the stone, in which this is certainly worthy of the highest admiration: that such a varied and complex account of events, as contained on this stone, could be encompassed within such a narrow space and using no more than one thousand and eighteen characters. There were, however, two interpretations made of this writing; the present one is very much in conformity with that which was made in <term>Beijing</term> <note>original: "Pequini"</note>, which is both more elegant and more appropriate to the <term>Chinese</term> <note>original: "Sinicæ"</note> phrasing. Although, for that same reason, it may appear less elegant in our own language, it is nonetheless most excellent; regarding its style and Chinese phrasing, it has been greatly praised by all those who profess themselves to be **Masters** of the said language.

<margin>At what time the Christian law was brought to China.</margin>
Furthermore, from this monument is gathered, first, the introduction of the Christian law into the Chinese kingdom, which occurred about a thousand years ago. Likewise, it shows with what great honor and veneration it was received by the **Emperors**; how, and through how many provinces it was promulgated; how much it flourished and spread during the 150 years of its greatest peak; and finally, what sort of persecutions it twice endured. It was so gradually suppressed by these trials that, had the knowledge of it not remained upon this monument, no further traces of it would survive. Certainly, in the **Chinese Chronicles**, scarcely anything is found regarding its introduction into **China** beyond the names of the aforementioned Kings and **Mandarins**.

But before I proceed further here, one difficulty yet remains to be resolved, which occurs concerning the year this stone was erected. <margin>Why was Alexander the Great called Dhul-Qarnayn?</margin>

Ribera, Tornielli, and others follow this view. # Chapter III. On the Coptic-Ethiopian Colonies

The Syro-Chaldean years, in all other respects, agree with the length and form of the Julian year, except that the intercalary day <note>A "leap day" added to keep the calendar in sync with the solar year.</note> in this era is added to the end of the month of <term>Shebat</term> <note>original: "Sabath"</note>, which corresponds to our February.

Having noted these things, we establish the beginnings of the Kingdom of the Greeks—following <term>Eusebius</term> <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian often called the "Father of Church History."</note>, <term>Scaliger</term> <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a foundational figure in the study of historical chronology.</note>, and others—in the 310th year before the era of Christ, during which the 117th <term>Olympiad</term> <note>A four-year period used by the ancient Greeks to mark time, beginning with the first Olympic Games.</note> occurred according to the *Alexandrian Chronicle*. For it is widely acknowledged that Alexander the Great died in the year when the 114th <term>Olympiad</term> began, in the final days of the month of <term>Hecatombaeon</term> <note>The first month of the ancient Attic calendar, roughly July.</note>, *as Plutarch writes*; namely, 322 years before the era of Christ (for Christ was born in the 3rd year, exclusive, of the 194th <term>Olympiad</term>). Therefore, the beginning of the "years of the Kingdom of the Greeks" differs from the elapsing years of Christ by 310 years; thus, in the first year of Christ, the 313th year of the Kingdom of the Greeks began.

From this it follows that if 310 is added to a given year of Christ, the result is the <margin>The Alexandrian Year</margin> Alexandrian year beginning in that passing year of Christ. If 310 is subtracted from an Alexandrian year, the remaining number is the year of Christ in which that Alexandrian year opens. Finally, if an Alexandrian year is subtracted from 310, the remaining number indicates the year before the era of Christ in which that Greek year began—or, the beginning of the <margin>Era of Dhul-Qarnayn.</margin> era of Alexander, the <note>original Arabic: تاريخ ذو القرنين, "Tarikh Dhul-Qarnayn"</note> "Era of the Two-Horned One," *as the Arabs and Egyptians call it.*

# CHAPTER IV.

## *On the Expedition of the Egyptians, or Copts, undertaken into India, China, and the remaining regions of Asia.*

<margin>
Colonies of the Coptic-Ethiopian Church.
</margin>
**S**ince in India, China, and other regions of Asia, numerous traces of the Christian Religion still exist to this day, I shall find it worth my effort—now that I have explained the <term>Syro-Coptic<note>original: "Syro-Coptitarum"; Kircher uses this term to suggest a collaborative mission between Syrian Christians and the Coptic Church of Egypt.</note></term> monument found in China—if I also show in this place by what occasion and route these Apostolic Men penetrated into such remote regions. For once this is accomplished, it will be clearly evident that Egypt was at all times a nursery <note>original: "Seminarium"; literally a seedbed or source.</note> not only for the promotion of the Christian Religion in foreign regions, but also for every superstition propagated throughout the whole world <note>Kircher frequently argued that Egypt was the cradle of both true religion and ancient pagan idolatry which spread to the East.</note>. But so that I may proceed more clearly in this obscure matter, it seemed best to first set forth the opinions of certain authors here, so that after these have been discussed, what should be determined regarding the matter at hand may become more lucid.

<margin>
Prester John.
</margin>
Therefore, first of all, there are those who assert that Christian colonies of this kind penetrated into China and the other regions of Asia by the aid of that great Asiatic Emperor, whom authors everywhere call <term>Prester John<note>A legendary Christian patriarch and king popular in European chronicles from the 12th to the 17th centuries, believed to rule a vast kingdom in the East.</note></term>. But since there is the greatest disagreement among authors concerning this Emperor, and the location, quality, and condition of his kingdoms...

### CHAPTER IV.
### On the Expedition of the Egyptians, or Copts, to India, etc.

...[multipli]cation and controversy, we shall first bring forward some points concerning himself and his kingdoms for a clearer explanation of things.

Just as the Kings of the Egyptians were first called Pharaohs, then Ptolemies; the Mauritanians <note>The people of the Maghreb in North Africa.</note> called *Seriphs* <note>original: "Seriphij"; referring to the Sharifs or rulers of Morocco.</note>; and the Persians formerly called *Xerxes* and *Artaxerxes*, and now called *Sophi* <note>original: "Sophi"; referring to the Safavid dynasty of Persia.</note>; so the name of **Prester John** has for a long time denoted the dignity of certain Christian Princes. 

<margin>
Where the Empire of Prester John is located.
</margin>
The more learned agree that these did not rule among the Ethiopians, or in any other part of Africa, as many wrongly suppose, but in Asia; however, exactly where he held his empire is not entirely certain. For what some have written—that they were the Kings of **Cathay**—makes the matter more doubtful, since in these recent years it has become known that whatever is called "Cathay" belongs to **China** <note>original: "Sinas"; the standard Latin term for the Chinese Empire.</note>, and there is no city or kingdom called by this name that is now found outside the borders of China. 

<margin>
What the Kingdom of Cathay is.
</margin>
Thus it was first discovered through geographical demonstration by **Matteo Ricci** <note>An influential Jesuit missionary (1552–1610) who mapped China and introduced Western science to the Ming court.</note> of the Society of Jesus, Superior among the Chinese, and afterwards sufficiently explored by **Bento de Góis** <note>A Jesuit explorer (1562–1607) whose overland journey from India to China proved that "Cathay" and "China" were the same landmass.</note> of the same Society, who set out from the **Mughal Empire** <note>original: "Regno Mogor"; the Persianate empire that ruled much of the Indian subcontinent.</note> and industriously investigated Cathay by a land route. I would not believe it far from the truth that there is no other region of the world, besides that part of the land found by our people within the limits of China, which is called by the name of Cathay.

These are not accustomed to do harm to the miners; but they wander in the shafts and tunnels: and though they do nothing, they seem to exercise themselves in every kind of labor; as if at one moment they were digging veins, at another pouring what has been excavated into vessels, and at another turning the hauling machine."

### Chapter IV. On the Coptic-Indian Expedition, etc.

The Apostolic King <note>original Arabic: *Melek alrassuli*</note> is called in the Ethiopic language <term>Negus Hawariawi</term> <note>literally "Apostolic King," from the Ethiopic ንግሥ ፡ ከወራዋዊ</note>. Joseph Scaliger argues that the fact that their Ethiopian Empire in Asia was once great and wide is evidenced by the "Ethiopian Crosses" which are seen in Japan, China <note>original: "Sina"</note>, and elsewhere. Furthermore, even the Temple of the Apostle Thomas located in the region of Maabar <note>A historical region on the Coromandel Coast of South India, famous in medieval accounts as the burial place of St. Thomas</note> possesses nothing that is not Ethiopian in its crosses, its architecture, many other things, and—what might surprise you—its very name. Thus far Scaliger's view. 

From this discourse, it is indeed well gathered that certain colonies were brought from Ethiopia into India, China, and other regions of Asia to propagate the Christian faith in those places, which is exactly what we are now striving to show. However, as for Scaliger's claim that Prester John <note>original: "Presbyterum Ioannem"</note> was African by origin, or that he was driven out of Asia and later settled in Ethiopia after gaining power there; this is entirely fabricated and, as we shall see later, lacks any foundation. For the greater part of the better authors agree with me that there were two distinct Emperors, one African and one Asian. 

The Empire of the Asian ruler flourished for many years, until <margin>Marco Polo the Venetian</margin> it reached a certain David. As Marco Polo the Venetian <note>original: "Paulus Marcus Venetus"</note> relates, this David was defeated in battle by a certain leader named Genghis <note>original: "Cinge," referring to Genghis Khan</note>. This Genghis, having been elected Emperor by the Scythians <note>A general term used by early modern writers for the Mongol and Tartar peoples</note>, began to be called "Prester Unc" <note>This likely refers to Toghrul, the Kerait leader known as Wang Khan, whom Genghis Khan defeated</note> in place of the former Priest-King. This battle resulted in a massive loss for the Christian cause and brought an end to the glory of that Empire and the title of Prester John in Asia. By what error, however, the name of Prester John was subsequently given to the Abyssinian <note>Ethiopian</note> Emperor...

### Chapter IV. On the Coptic-Indian Expedition, etc.

<margin>
Why the Emperor of the Abyssinians is also called Prester John.
</margin>
I make the matter clear. At the time when the Portuguese <note>original: *Lusitani*</note> were exploring new regions of the world by sea, the name of **Prester John** was celebrated throughout Europe with great renown. It was said that he was a most powerful Emperor, lord of many kingdoms, and Christian by religion, though his exact location remained unknown. 

Therefore, Pêro da Covilhã <note>original: *Petrus Couillanius*, a Portuguese explorer and diplomat</note>—whom King **John II of Portugal** had sent to investigate this prince, traveling first across the Mediterranean Sea and then by land—heard while he was in "Asian India" (where he had arrived) that there was a very powerful prince in the Ethiopia located below Egypt who professed the Christian religion. He traveled to meet this ruler; and when he found many things about him that matched the persistent rumors that had spread among Europeans regarding the true Prester John, he believed that this was indeed the man called Prester John. 

He, therefore, was the first to begin calling the **Abyssinian Emperor** by that name. Others who entered Ethiopia in the following years followed his example and easily carried this same error back into Europe. Thus, when we speak of Prester John, we by no means mean the Abyssinian Emperor; for, aside from the fact that his empire is separated from the Asian one by the "whole of the heavens" <note>a Latin idiom, *toto coelo*, meaning they are poles apart or entirely different</note>, there is also no mention in the chronology of the Kings of Ethiopia (as is evident from the Latin version held in the Vatican) of his or from...

...they would have it that he suffered; it will become clear that this error crept in from a poor understanding of the word **Calamina** <note>original: *Calamina*; a traditional name in Christian hagiography for the place where St. Thomas was martyred</note>, once we reveal what place was properly **Calamina**.

<margin>**Calurmina** is not a city separate from **Meliapore**.</margin>
Note, therefore, that according to the **Malabar Chronicle**, no city of this name is found in **India** today, nor was one found in the past; instead of **Calamina**, one should read ***Calurmina***,

<margin>It is composed of *Calur* and *Mina*. This means "upon the rock."</margin>
which is established as a **Malabaric** word <note>Referring to the local languages of the Malabar Coast, such as Malayalam or Tamil</note>, composed of *Calur* and *mina*; the latter signifies "above" and the former "rock," as if to say "upon the rock." Moreover, at **Meliapore** <note>Mylapore, now a neighborhood in Chennai, India</note>, in that place where the Holy Apostle is said to have suffered martyrdom, there is a certain huge rock, which to this day they call *Calur* in the **Malabar** tongue. Therefore, when the **Malabar** annals relate that he suffered at ***Calurmina***, they by no means understood by that word a particular city, but rather the rock called *Calur* near **Meliapore**, which the Apostle used to climb daily for the sake of prayer, and upon which, while he was intent on prayer, he was afterwards killed. # Chapter IV. On the Coptic-Indian Expedition, etc.

# Chapter IV. On the Coptic-Indian Expedition, etc.

He <note>Referring to Osiris, whose travels were discussed on the previous page.</note> built quite a few cities for the Indians, one of which he named **Nysa**, wishing to leave a monument to that **Nysa in Egypt** where he had been raised. In this **Indian Nysa**, he planted ivy, which grows and survives there more than in any other place in **India** or its neighboring lands. Furthermore, he left many other signs of his arrival in those territories. Led by these signs, later **Indians** have stirred up a controversy regarding this God, contending that he was of the Indian nation; following in his footsteps, it is highly probable that **Egyptians** visited these regions more frequently in later times.

<margin>The philosophers of the Indians drew all their knowledge from the Egyptians.</margin>
Certainly, the **Persian Magi**, the **Indian Brahmans**, as well as other wise men of **Asia**, received their entire system of philosophy and all their rites and ceremonies concerning the worship of the Gods from the **Egyptians** through this mutual commerce. This is not only clearly taught by **Philostratus** <note>A Greek scholar (c. 170–250 CE) who wrote the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, a biography of a famous wandering philosopher.</note> in his *Life of Apollonius*; indeed, the very customs and habits of the said nations point to this brilliantly. To this very day, we can see the worship of the **Sun, Moon, Stars, Earth, and Animals** of every kind flourishing in **India, China, Japan, Tartary** (or **Cathay**), and even in **America** itself, just as it did in **Egypt** from time immemorial.

<margin>Egyptian idolatry still flourishes everywhere throughout all of India.</margin>

Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who wrote extensively on the life of Joseph.</note> teaches in his book *On Joseph* that this Egyptian word should be understood in this way.

Oleaster <note>Jerónimo Aznar de Oleaster (d. 1563), a Portuguese Dominican scholar and commentator on the Pentateuch.</note> seems to have held this opinion <margin>Oleaster, drawing from Rabbi Iarchi <note>Rashi</note>, in his commentary on Genesis.</margin> in his commentary on this passage, having been persuaded by Hebrew books. *It seems to me,* he says, *that if the words Zaphenath-paneah are Hebrew, there is no doubt that the first,* <note>original Hebrew: צפנת</note> *Zaphenath, signifies "hidden," from* <note>original Hebrew: צפן</note> *tsaphan, which means to hide or conceal. Anyone who has now diligently compared the words presented in these paradigms will see that there is indeed a great affinity among the Oriental languages cited here for one another; but for Coptic, there is none at all. For what relation <note>original Latin: "obtineat"</note> the words *the father* <note>original Coptic: ⲡⲓⲱⲧ (*pi-iot*)</note> and *the son* <note>original Coptic: ⲡⲓϣⲏⲣⲓ (*pi-shiri*)</note> have to *Ab ben*, *Abo uabro*, *Ab ubnu*, *wawalda* <note>these are the transliterations of "father" and "son" from the Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic examples on the previous page</note> and others of this kind, I can hardly discern. 

Added to this is the fact that Theseus <note>referring to Teseo Ambrogio, a 16th-century linguist who published a famous polyglot introduction to languages</note> wrongly concludes the affinity of languages from one or two words. For by this reasoning, I might say German is most closely related to Hebrew, or even to Persian, since it contains many names proper to the said languages. By a similar reasoning, one would act imprudently who, from a very few Armenian words—for example, *Gurcustan* <note>Armenian: Գուրճստան, meaning Georgia</note>, *Tataristan* <note>Armenian: Թաթարստան, meaning Tartary</note>, *Turkistan* <note>Armenian: Թուրքստան, meaning Turkey</note>, and *Shahstan* <note>Armenian: շահստան, likely referring to a royal city or province</note>, words with which the Indians and Armenians indicate Georgia, Tartary, Turkey, and Armenia—would therefore conclude that the Indian language is related to Armenian. In truth, there is hardly any language that does not borrow certain words from others, even if they themselves are entirely different from one another. But let these things be said regarding the name *Psontomphanech* <note>This refers to Zaphenath-Paaneah, the Egyptian name given to Joseph in Genesis 41:45; Kircher is using it as an example of an Egyptian word whose etymology had been debated.</note>.

Since this word is Coptic or Egyptian, as—besides the authors to be cited shortly—Holy Scripture certainly indicates clearly with these words:

But the remaining days they call **mentepi-terpin epagomenas** <note>original Coptic: ⲙⲉⲛⲧⲉⲡⲓⲧⲉⲣⲡⲓⲛ ⲉⲡⲁⲅⲟⲙⲉⲛⲁⲥ</note> or intercalary days.

<margin>On the nature of the ancient Coptic and Egyptian year.</margin>
It should be noted, therefore, that in ancient times, especially among the Egyptians, although the year consisted of only 360 days (a number most suitable because of the ease of dividing it), it was by no means a completely perfect year corresponding to the <term>Zodiac</term> <note>the belt of constellations through which the sun appears to move</note>. For this reason, the Egyptian <term>Hierophants</term> <note>priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note>, knowing that the common year lacked five whole days and a quarter for perfection, would express that perfect year through a <term>Hieroglyph</term> whenever they wished to signify it: a Serpent coiled into a sphere and a circle, biting its tail with its mouth; as if the Sun would not complete a perfect and absolute course of the Zodiac if those five days were missing. They called this Serpent **Nesi**; the Copts and the most ancient Egyptian Christians retain this word today, and they are accustomed to call the <term>epagomenal days</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπαγομένας; the five "added" days that round out the 360-day calendar to 365</note> *Nesi* in the ancient Egyptian or Coptic language, which we are currently discussing. For thus the Coptic <term>Onomasticon</term> <note>a dictionary of names and terms</note> speaks of them.

<margin>A serpent biting its tail, coiled in a circle, is called *Nisi* in Egyptian, by which name the Copts call the epagomenal days.</margin>
<margin>Coptic-Arabic Onomasticon, folio 55, regarding the Coptic months:</margin>
The Coptic months: their year is three hundred and sixty-five
days: five are the *Nesi*, and the leap-year day occurs every four years. 
The beginning of the year is the *Nauruz* <note>Nawruz</note>, which is a Persian word.

Every four years, after the completion [of the year], is the Nowruz, and it is a Persian word. <note>original: "col arba Sanin badu alfanee ilnuruz voahi lephath pharfieh." This is Kircher's transliteration of Arabic explaining the Coptic New Year, known as Nayrouz.</note>

The months of the Copts are twelve, and their year contains three hundred and sixty-five days. Five days, called **Nesi**, are intercalated every fourth year. The beginning of the year is **Neuruz** <note>Nayrouz</note>, which is a Persian word. <margin>In Horus, the Serpent is called *Misi*. You should read *Nisi* instead of the corrupted *Misi*.</margin> Horus <note>Kircher refers to Horapollo, the purported author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note> also writes that the Serpent, fashioned **in the form of the world** <note>original Greek: Κοσμοειδῶς ἐσχηματισμένον</note>, by which they signified the Year, the World, the King, and other things, is called *Mesi*; but he writes this corruptly, as many other things occur corruptly in Horus's work. For it is clear from the words cited a little earlier that the Copts even now call the end of the Solar year *Nesi*. Furthermore, the name <margin>The cause and origin of the **epagomenal** days.</margin> **epagomenal** <note>original Greek: ἐπαγομένων; the five extra days added to the 360-day calendar to align it with the solar year</note> is used **by way of privation** <note>original Greek: κατ’ στέρησιν; suggesting something was "missing" or "taken away"</note>, as if the year had once simply been 360 days. As I have said, the <term>Hierophants</term> <note>priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note> themselves not only had this written in their books, but they also added a myth regarding the origin and cause of **the epagomenal days** <note>original Greek: τῶν ἐπαγομένων</note>. They said that Mercury, playing at dice with the Moon, won, and extorted from her the seventy-second part of the year, which he afterwards added to the 360 days—which was the measure of the ancient year. <margin>Plutarch, in the book *On Isis and Osiris*, near the beginning.</margin> Plutarch tells the story in this way: They say that Rhea came secretly into the embrace of Saturn; soon she also had relations with the Sun, but as if condemned for her pregnancy, she found neither a year nor a month in which to give birth. Mercury, also seized with love for her, lay with her. Thereupon, playing at **astragals** <note>original: Astragalis; ancient dice made of knuckle-bones</note> with the Moon, he took away the seventieth part of each day, from which he fashioned the five days...

### Chapter V. Whether the Coptic Language is Truly Egyptian.

An **aroura** <note>original Latin: *aruum*; a unit of land area used in ancient Egypt</note> is said to be a measure of land encompassing one hundred cubits. Therefore, when they wish to say "a year," they say "a fourth." This is because, as they report, from one rising of the star to which we have given the name **Sothis** <note>original Greek: **Σώθις**; the star Sirius</note> (in Coptic, **Sioti** <note>original Coptic: **Ⲥⲓⲱϯ**</note>) to the next, a fourth part of a day is interposed. For indeed, the Year of God (meaning the Sun) is completed in 365 days. For this reason, the Egyptians also calculate and <term>intercalate</term> <note>the insertion of an extra day into the calendar</note> an extra day every fourth year; since four quarters of a day complete one full day. <margin>Pliny, Book 2</margin> This is confirmed by Eudoxus <note>a Greek astronomer who studied in Egypt</note> in the works of Pliny; whose *lustrum* <note>a period of years</note> is nothing other than the four-year **Canicular cycle** <note>a cycle based on the rising of the "Dog Star," Sirius</note>, just as the Coptic calculation shows itself to be a perfect match to the ancient Egyptian calculation regarding these years. We shall speak of this more extensively at the end of this little work, where you will also find explained what the Copts mean by **Neuruz** <note>Nairuz, the Coptic New Year festival, derived from the Persian word for "New Day"</note>.

<margin>Pausanias in *Arcadia*</margin> It is clear, therefore, from what has been said, that the Copts have handed down to the present day not only the names of the ancient Egyptian months and the *Nisi* <note>likely a reference to the intercalary days or a specific term for "added" days</note>, or "added days" <note>original Greek: **ἐπαγομένων** (epagomenon); five extra days added to the 360-day year</note>, but also the entire system for establishing the ecclesiastical calendar received from their ancestors. That the Coptic months are the same as the Egyptian ones is abundantly demonstrated not only by our *Onomasticon* <note>a book of names or specialized vocabulary</note> but also by the other authors whom we cite below. Indeed, Pausanias reports that in the month of **Paopi** <note>original Greek: **Παοπι**</note>, Osiris returned from a long journey. # Chapter V. Whether the Coptic Language is Truly Egyptian.

...[discre]pant change, corrupted as the centuries followed. <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page: "lest perhaps, on account of the somewhat discrepant change..."</note>

<margin>Among the Copts, no name of the Gods remains except **Phtha**.</margin>

Furthermore, one might deservedly wonder why among the **Egyptian Copts** there is no talk of the names of the Pagan Gods <note>original Latin: "Gentilium Deorum"</note>, except for the single name ***Phtha*** (concerning whom we shall speak in the following chapter). For I have never discovered a mention in their books of the names of **Osiris**, **Isis**, **Horus**, **Ichto**, **Emeph**, or others cited by **Plutarch** <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 46–120 AD) whose work *On Isis and Osiris* is a major source for Egyptian myth</note> and **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note>, even though I have always investigated this with singular zeal. 

While this rendered me much perplexed and wavering in mind, I finally discovered that this did not occur because the Copts were ignorant of such names, but because, moved by the love of the highest religion <note>Kircher refers here to the Coptic transition to Christianity</note>, they thought it a divine sin to profane the sacred histories—in the writing of which they were entirely occupied—with the fabulous names of the Pagan Gods. In this, they imitate the **Hebrews**, who also seem to have suppressed such names with deep silence; this was partly because it was never permitted for the Egyptians to mix with the Hebrews, and partly due to the supreme detestation of idolatry and foreign servitude. They pursued this with such hatred that they considered it a crime to be expiated by death even to utter the name of a false deity with one's mouth. And this is the reason why they considered it reckless to touch upon not only the names, but even the histories themselves of those deeds once performed in Egypt by the Heroes and their ancestors, regarding them as harmful to tender minds. But what should be thought concerning the **Coptic** name for God, let us now reveal.

<header>Chapter VI. On the Name of the God Phtha.</header>

# Chapter VI. On the Name of the God Phtha.

...[how much] faith should be placed <note>This continues the thought from the previous page regarding the reliability of certain linguistic theories</note>; I certainly, who have striven with the greatest zeal to investigate the truth of this matter from the monuments of the **Copts**, have indeed very frequently read the name of God as **P-nouti** <note>original: ΠΝΟΥ†</note>; but **Ph-nouti** <note>original: ΦΝΟΥ†</note>—which they say is equivalent to the contracted form **Phtha** <note>original: Φ†</note>—I do not remember ever reading in any of the Coptic monuments. From this fact alone it is clearly evident that **Phtha** is entirely different from the name of God **Ph-nouti**, or more correctly, **P-nouti**. 

Even if it were granted, though not conceded, that **Phtha** is the same as **P-nouti**, it by no means follows that in its abbreviated form it must necessarily be pronounced as **P-nouti** rather than **Phtha**. For no one is ignorant that it is the custom of most Eastern peoples to pronounce abbreviated names—of whatever sort, for the sake of greater brevity—exactly as they are written in their shortened form. I shall make the matter clearer with some examples: <term>P-O-S</term> <note>original: $\overline{Πoc}$, a Coptic contraction of "Pichoeis"</note> is an abbreviated name of God among the Copts, which is the same as *Lord*. Yet it has no other pronunciation than that which the letters themselves give. **Agla** and **Haba** <note>Hebrew: אגלה and חבה</note> are abbreviated names of God among the **Hebrews**; these result from the letters which they call <margin>Heads of words.</margin> <note>original: Rasche theboth (Roshei Tevot). This refers to the use of acronyms where the first letter of each word in a phrase forms a new word.</note> **Agla**, for instance, is formed from the first letters of the words in the following sentence:

->**A**tah  **G**ibor  **L**eolam  **A**donai<-

->that is<-

->You are strong forever, O Lord.<-

<header>Chapter VI. On the Name of the God Phtha.</header>

## *Chapter VI. On the Name of the God Phtha.*

*Haba* <note>An abbreviated name for God used in mystical traditions</note> actually arises from this phrase: **The Holy One, blessed is He** <note>Hebrew: *Kadosh Baruch Hu* (קדוש ברוך הוא)</note>; yet when these names are mentioned, they are not pronounced in an expanded way, but in a contracted form, as those skilled in this language know. I could bring forward here countless similar examples from the **Hebrews**, **Arabs**, **Syrians**, and **Persians**, if the truth now revealed required more detailed demonstrations, or if the haste of the *Prodromus* <note>Kircher refers to the rapid preparation of his book *Prodromus Coptus* (1636)</note> permitted it. It stands, therefore, that abbreviated names of God are not necessarily pronounced in their expanded form.

Others, however, who assert that this name **Ph-t** <note>original: Φ-†</note>—on the grounds that the letter † <note>The Coptic letter "Dei" or "Ti"</note> sounds like a "D" rather than a "Th" (Θ)—should therefore be pronounced not as **Phtha** but as **Phda**, are similarly mistaken. For it is obvious that this last letter of the **Coptic** Alphabet, †, corresponds entirely in equivalent sound to the mystical **Thau** <note>The letter Tav</note> of the **Hebrews** and **Samaritans**, and the **Theta** (Θ) of the **Greeks**. However, the fact that the Egyptian **Copts** everywhere pronounce it like a "D" should be considered as occurring not because of its natural pronunciation, but because of a defect of the tongue <note>Kircher suggests that the local accent changed the original sound</note> with which the **Copts** struggle when pronouncing this letter †.

But others will say that it is improbable that the Egyptian Christians used this profane name of a pagan god for the name of the true God. To these we respond: this name **Phtha** <note>original: Φ-†</note> was one of the absolute names of God, just as **Thoth**, **Emeph**, and **Ichtho** <note>Names used in Hermetic and Egyptian theology to describe aspects of the Divine</note> were also names that explained certain effects of God.

<summary>Kircher argues that the Coptic abbreviation for God should be pronounced "Phtha" rather than expanded into "P-nouti," comparing it to how Hebrew abbreviations are spoken. He also addresses why Christian Copts might have retained a name originally associated with a pagan deity.</summary>

...and such names as among the Hebrews: **Jehovah** <note>Hebrew: יהוה</note>, **The Place** <note>Hebrew: *Makom* (מקום), a Rabbinic title for God implying His omnipresence</note>, **The Name** <note>Hebrew: *Shem* (שם)</note>, **Lord** <note>Hebrew: *Adonai* (אדני)</note>, and **God** <note>Hebrew: *El* (אל)</note>; and among the Arabs, **Allah** <note>Arabic: الله</note>; and therefore, the **Copts** should not be blamed at all if they retained that name of God along with the language of the ancient **Egyptians**. Having prefaced these points, let us now finally reveal what that name of God, **Phtha** <note>original: Φ-☥</note>, properly is, where it is derived from, what mysteries it refers to, or of what thing it is a **Hieroglyphic** <term>Hieroglyphic: A sacred symbol or character used in ancient Egyptian writing to represent a concept or sound</term>. I say, therefore, that the **Copts** <note>the Christian descendants of the ancient Egyptians</note>, having received this name of God, **Phtha**, from the Ancients, counted it among the secret and mysterious names of God. To understand this, one must know that the nature of mystical names once required that they be distinguished by certain characters or **monograms** <term>Monogram: A motif of two or more letters overlapping</term>, so that they would not be profaned by being mixed with more common words; we read that this was customary among the **Hebrews**, **Chaldeans**, and **Arabs** more than other nations. They not only wrote the name of God mystically, but also forbade writing it openly or pronouncing it recklessly under the heaviest penalty. ### *Concerning the affinity of the Coptic language, or Egyptian, to the Greek, and its corruption occurring over the course of time.*

<margin>
The figure for the number six <note>original: *senarius*</note> among the Greeks is ϛ; among the Copts, it occupies the sixth place among the letters.
</margin>

**T**he closeness which Coptic—or ancient Egyptian—maintains with the Greek language is such that it can hardly be discerned whether the former flowed from the latter, or the latter from the former. Hence, we might not wrongly call it the most ancient Greek. For it is probable—if we believe Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, Roman naturalist and author</note> and Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian and bishop</note>—that Egyptian was first transported into Greece along with the letters by Cadmus and Phoenix <note>Mythical figures credited with bringing the alphabet from the East to Greece</note> after the flood of Deucalion <note>The Great Flood in Greek mythology, similar to the story of Noah</note>, where it gave birth to a daughter, namely the Greek language. Indeed, that the Greeks also received the method of counting by letters from the Egyptians is sufficiently shown by the Coptic letter <term>So</term> <note>original: ⲋ</note>, which, just as it holds the sixth place in the order of letters, is also the indicator for the number six. This the Greeks also use to this day as the figure <term>stigma</term> <note>original: ϛ, a ligature of sigma and tau used to represent the number 6</note> for the number six, and it has no other use outside of numbers. This is a clear sign that the Egyptian language established a new colony in Greece; which, afterwards gradually refined, shortly [achieved] immense growth...

This is also what Sixtus of Siena <note>Sixtus Senensis, a 16th-century Franciscan scholar and theologian</note> seems to suggest; he says that most of the books of Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical Egyptian sage to whom many philosophical and alchemical works were attributed</note> seem to be written in a Greek style. Whatever the case, certainly the Greek language was in use among the Egyptians, as evidenced by the expeditions of many philosophers to Egypt and the continuous exchange of literature on both sides. This would not have happened unless they used some common language, just as Europeans use Latin. ## Chapter VII: On the Affinity of the Coptic Language to the Greek

Furthermore, since nothing in the nature of things is found to be stable or firm, but instead everything is found to be fluid and deceptive, it is indeed not surprising if—just as in all other languages—the greatest changes occurred in Coptic over the course of time. For nothing is more subject to change than languages, as both others and the most learned Father Melchior Inchofer <note>Melchior Inchofer (1584–1648) was a Jesuit scholar and contemporary of Kircher who wrote on the history of the Latin language</note> showed most excellently in his *History of Sacred Latin*; indeed, all the kingdoms of the West demonstrate this abundantly. 

For who today knows the ancient language of the Etruscans? Who can easily distinguish the ancient idioms of the Saxons, the Vandals, and other nations from those of today? Certainly, inscriptions show how much the modern Etruscan and Latin languages have receded from the ancient ones: both the Iguvine Tablets <note>original: tabulae Eugubinae; a set of seven bronze tablets discovered in 1444, crucial for the study of the Umbrian language, though Kircher here identifies them as Etruscan</note>, written in the ancient letters and language of the Etruscans and approaching the Hebrew manner of speaking more than the Latin; and the *rostrate* <note>meaning: columns adorned with the prows, or "rostra," of captured enemy ships, such as the Column of Gaius Duilius, which bore very archaic Latin inscriptions</note> columns, which have not yet been fully explored by anyone. 

How many corruptions of languages arise from the neighboring assembly of diverse nations, we are taught by the Italians, Gauls, Dalmatians, Istrians, and Slavs bordering Germany; their dialects are so confused by the peculiarities <note>original: idiotismis</note> of these nations that many, speaking a mixed language, seem to speak nothing at all. The ancient language of the Carthaginians <note>original: Poenorum</note> also degenerated so much from the Hebrew and Syrian <note>meaning: Syriac or Aramaic</note>—with which it was once the same, as Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 342–420 AD), the Church Father and biblical translator</note> testifies—that it can scarcely be recognized. Regarding the Greek language, if you consider only the bare vocabulary, the Coptic language seems deservedly to claim much of it for itself. However, if you look at the syntax and the construction of nouns, Coptic will seem just as far removed from Greek as it is near to it in its vocabulary. 

<margin>
The Coptic language is related to Greek in its vocabulary, but not in the syntax of its nouns.
</margin>

For Coptic is so different and distinct <note>original: *deformis*, here meaning "differently formed" or "unlike in shape"</note> not only from Greek, but also from all other languages in its method of declining nouns and conjugating verbs, that—if you except a few instances—it seems to agree with no other language in any respect at all.
