### Chapter VII: On the Affinity of the Coptic Language to Greek

...[has] a great affinity to the Greek language; however, if you look at the syntax, you will find a remarkable difference. Therefore, when we spoke earlier about its affinity to the Greek language, I would like you to understand that this refers by no means to the syntax, but only to the vocabulary taken in its simplest form. Furthermore, without any regard for punctuation or word separation, the Copts heap the words of a sentence together in such a way that they seem to intend to form a single word. This is evident in the following sentences:

<margin>The Coptic language is difficult</margin>

**The word was made flesh** <note>Coptic: ΠΣΑΧΙ ΑϤΕΡ ΟΥΣΑΡΞ; original Latin: *Verbum caro factum est.*</note>

and that phrase:

**This is the disciple of Jesus** <note>Coptic: ΦΑΙ ΠΕ ΠΜΑΘΗΤΗΣ ΝΙΗΣ; original Latin: *hic est Discipulus ille Iesu.*</note>

Also:

**God is the true judge** <note>Coptic: Φϯ ΟΥΚΡΙΤΗΣ ΜΗΙ ΠΕ; original Latin: *Deus Iudex verus ille.*</note>

According to our way of writing, these ought to be written like this:

**The Word was flesh** <note>original: *Verbum fuit caro.*</note>
**God is the true judge**, etc.

And indeed, in these arrangements of words, if you set aside a few specific terms, one finds neither clarity in the sentences nor any <term>Hellenism</term> <note>original: *hellenismos*; here meaning the imitation of Greek grammatical rules or style</note> in the construction. Whether this intricate and irregular method of constructing sentences in the Coptic language was the same as that of the ancient language of the Egyptians is entirely difficult to assert, especially since we currently lack books written in the ancient, pure language of the Egyptians. It is probable, however, and as much as one can gather from the monuments of the Copts, va—

...from the comparison of earlier <note>original: *superiorum*</note> authors and ancient readings. It has been possible to gather that the ancient language—if not exactly the same, as it has been corrupted by the passage of time—was at least not entirely unlike Coptic, which flowed from it and still retains a large part of the vocabulary proper to the ancient tongue. Truly, so that something certain might be established concerning this, Egypt itself would need to be consulted. One would have to see if perhaps some traces of it might still be found in the ancient ruins of the pyramids; if such evidence were available, it would not be difficult to arrive at a knowledge of its properties through a comparison made with Coptic. But since there is a lack of those who might unearth such lost antiquities with tireless zeal, it is no wonder they remain inaccessible in this age. Nothing remains to us except a few fragments, as if salvaged from the shipwreck of time; a few words, I say, noted by ancient authors, with which we may console our lack of knowledge <note>original: *inopiam nostram*, literally "our poverty"</note>.

### Chapter VIII. On the Utility of the Coptic Language

...perfectly reach the difficulties of literature; or overcome them once they are perceived. For we see that while we are in doubt, innumerable books are indeed encountered, which nevertheless, if you weigh them well, you will find scarcely one in a thousand that can be of assistance to minds established in perplexity. Indeed, it is shameful to say, all writers so conspire in the words of one another that if you remove the disguise of words, you find the same thing entirely written, endorsed, and transcribed. Hence, I judge it happens that, in the manner of linked blind men with one drawing the other, all fall into the abyss <note>original: *barathrum*, referring to a deep pit or metaphorical "maw" of errors</note> of uncorrectable errors. I do not think there is any other cause for this literary calamity than the neglect of foreign literatures and arts. Because these are mostly learned with the greatest labor, certain people flee to that shameful asylum of laziness, trying to veil their sluggishness and poverty of mind. They badly use that phrase "to what good?" <note>Latin: *cui bono*—a common rhetorical question asking what the practical benefit of a study is</note> as a pretext for their own disgrace, as if nothing is profitable except that from which the belly and the purse <note>original: *marsupium*, a small pouch for coins</note> might swell.

Truly, I have a far different mind, a different spirit toward letters. I am so prepared by nature that I consider nothing worthier of a noble man than to test one’s industry and the powers of the intellect <note>original: *ingenium*, referring to innate talent or creative power</note>, especially in restoring those things which either forgetful or unlearned ages have neglected over the course of time; or in sagaciously searching out what nature has hidden in her more secret inner chambers; so indeed that all of this—

...of this kind, so that I might survey hidden treasures; and even if I might be less able to export them, at the very least I might wallow in them in the manner of Alcmaeon <note>original: *Alcmæonis*. Therefore, let us proceed to the Coptic language, which—if you except Hebrew—is not undeservedly the most ancient of languages. It ought to be doubtful to no one that from its restoration a huge utility and benefit can arise, both for literature and for the Church. ...save for our *Thesaurus*, or Coptic *onomasticon* <note>original: *onomastici*. A Greek-derived term for a dictionary of names or specialized terms.</note>, in which the technical terms of all branches of knowledge and sciences are set forth with such precision in Coptic words that, in this regard, it seems to yield to no other language. Moreover, it is not believable that terms of this kind were merely invented by the author of the *onomasticon*; rather, they were drawn from the authors of various disciplines and collected with the utmost diligence. I am certainly led by many reasons—which I shall present elsewhere—to believe that those famous volumes of Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom ancient Egyptian-Greek wisdom and "Hermetic" texts were attributed.</note> were written in no other language but Coptic. Who then does not see that great benefits can arise for the Republic of Letters <note>original: *Reip: literariæ* (Respublica Literaria). The pan-European community of scholars.</note> from the restoration of this language? It is of great value to the Church indeed, because the most ancient Church of the Egyptian Christians uses this language in its sacred rites—even though it is almost entirely unknown to the people themselves at this present time—and it possesses all the Codices of both the Old and New Testaments written in this same tongue. Furthermore, it preserves the first four Councils <note>The Ecumenical Councils (Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon) which defined early Christian doctrine.</note> and many other works pertaining to ecclesiastical matters, as we have also reviewed above. # *Chapter VIII. On the Utility of the Coptic Language*

...our Coptic-Arabic **Thesaurus**, <note>The text begins with "rus," the end of the word "Thesaurus" from the previous page.</note> (which the most illustrious gentleman Pietro della Valle, <note>Pietro della Valle (1586–1652) was a famous Italian traveler who brought important manuscripts back from the Near East.</note> a Roman Patrician, shared with me to be translated out of his outstanding passion for the restoration of Oriental languages, having not long ago brought it from Egypt) seemed, above all others, worthy of being published without delay due to the abundance of subjects, names, and words with which it is filled. This said Thesaurus, translated by us from the Arabic and Coptic languages into Latin, consists primarily of three parts. The first part claims for itself those things which pertain to Grammar. The second contains the names of things distributed into certain classes or subjects, which we, following Junius <note>likely referencing the scholar Franciscus Junius</note> not incorrectly, call an <term>Onomasticon</term> <note>a vocabulary organized by topic (like a thesaurus) rather than alphabetically</note> or Nomenclator. Finally, the third part completes the work with individual words occurring throughout Coptic monuments, arranged according to alphabetical order; for this reason we call it a dictionary, though the Copts call it the *Chosen Scale* <note>original Latin: "Scalam Electam"; in Arabic: "al-Sullam al-Mukhtar"</note>, a most fitting name. For in this work, individual words are organized according to their endings, using a method entirely contrary to the order of our own dictionaries. For just as among us the search for words is initiated from the capital <note>starting</note> letters, so among the Copts, the search for words must be conducted from the final letters of the terms. This is a method that the *Qamus* <note>The "Al-Qamus al-Muhit," a famous 14th-century Arabic dictionary by al-Fayruzabadi</note>, the celebrated Arabic dictionary, also observes.

### Chapter VIII. On the Utility of the Coptic Language

<margin>Interpreters of Holy Scripture.</margin>
Therefore, this Coptic-Arabic-Latin **Thesaurus** of ours is filled with such a wealth of words and names that I believe there is no circle of scholars to whom it will not bring the greatest utility. First, interpreters of Holy Scripture will find in it a remarkable abundance of subjects and names specific to their field, which will assist them with the obscure names occurring in the sacred texts. <margin>Physicians</margin> With the help of this work, physicians will be rescued from various uncertainties that frequently arise regarding the names of plants, minerals, and other medicines explained here in Coptic, Arabic, and Latin. <margin>Astronomers.</margin> Astronomers will soon look upon the heavenly host of stars and see individual stars honored with their ancient names, with which the first inventors of astronomy—the Egyptians and Arabs—once designated them. <margin>Natural Philosophers.</margin> <note>original: "Physici"; in this period, the term refers to "Natural Philosophers" or scientists who study the natural world rather than modern medical physicists.</note> Nor will material be lacking for natural philosophers to refine their subjects of study. For they will contemplate with the greatest joy the names of elements, stones, trees, plants, four-legged animals, birds, fish, and serpents, just as they were identified by the Ancients. <margin>Mathematicians.</margin> Mathematicians will also find ancient technical terms of the arts in geometry, statics, arithmetic, astronomy, music, and similar arts and sciences, each one marked with its Coptic, Arabic, and Latin names. <margin>Antiquarians</margin> Finally, for antiquarians, this work will be nothing other than a storehouse <note>original: "promus condus," a Latin idiom for a steward or a cellarer who both stores and brings out supplies.</note> from which innumerable benefits to literature will soon flow out from

...they will experience. And these are the Coptic books that have come to my attention.

Not long ago, a certain acquaintance brought forward various <term>inscriptions</term>—found, as he claimed, among Coptic or Egyptian <term>Codices</term> <note>handwritten books or manuscripts</note>—written in that <term>character</term> <note>script or alphabet</note> which some people wrongly call "the Script of Solomon." Once I had unraveled these inscriptions with the help of the analytical art <note>referring to the skill of deciphering or cryptanalysis</note>—and with no great effort—I discovered that both the meaning of said inscriptions and the phrasing (which in many ways differed from the Arabic style of writing) bore the appearance of some kind of fraud. Consequently, I could in no way be persuaded to believe that these "characters of Solomon" were ever used by the Copts. Furthermore, no traces of them are to be found in Coptic monuments, nor among other reliable authors under this name. Therefore, lest I cause trouble for anyone by touching this "apple of discord," <note>original: "Eridis pomum"; a reference to the mythological golden apple that caused the Trojan War, used here to mean a controversial or divisive topic.</note> I judged that their explanations should be intentionally omitted. 

I am aware that many characters and inscriptions of this sort <note>original: "huius farinae," literally "of this flour" or "of this grain"</note> are circulated far and wide under the name of Solomon. However, I am unwilling to place much faith in them, since they smell of some counterfeit birth and seem to have been produced in the workshop of idle troublemakers <note>original: "maleferiatorum hominum," referring to people who use their leisure time for mischief or forgery</note> rather than that of Solomon. 

Because some people desire my judgment concerning this type of <term>character</term>, I say that a <term>character</term> of this sort is by no means Solomon's, since it is purely Arabic...

...it might be, and that in later times it flowed forth from the chirographic, or cursive <term>Hebrew character</term> <note>a style of handwritten Hebrew script</note> (as we will clearly demonstrate elsewhere); but I have discovered from various inscriptions on coins that it actually belongs to the <term>Agarenes</term> <note>a historical term for Arabs, derived from the biblical Hagar</note>, or the Saracens of Africa. For the sake of <term>calligraphy</term> <note>original Greek: καλλιγραφίας; the art of beautiful writing</note>, these people were once accustomed to use Arabic letters drawn with deliberate care above lines as if they were <term>concatenated</term> <note>linked or chained together in a continuous flow</note>. This is abundantly testified by that most celebrated Arabic inscription which Georgio Gualterio <note>a 17th-century Italian antiquarian known for his work on Sicilian inscriptions</note> presents in his *Antiquities of Sicily* at the Church of Saint Restituta; it is visible on a certain marble, most elegantly joined together in a continuous line. However, since many inscriptions made in this character are circulated here and there, it seemed appropriate to set down the alphabet of said characters in this place—especially since I know of no one else who has provided it yet. Thus, if inscriptions of this kind should ever fall into the hands of someone skilled in the Arabic language (as they have not infrequently fallen into mine), he might find here a key by which he can more easily penetrate its inner meanings.

## *A true, certain, and faithful interpretation of a wonderful and most ancient inscription, carved into a certain rock of Mount Horeb, which is part of Mount Sinai, explained by no one before now.*

While I was preparing the <term>Egyptian Forerunner</term> <note>original: *Prodromum AEgyptiacum*; Kircher’s 1636 work which was his first major publication on Coptic and Egyptian studies</note>,
and while various riddles and various hieroglyphic
knots were being presented to me by various people to be unraveled;
among others, the Reverend Father
Dominicus Germanus—a Silesian by birth,
professor of the Arabic language, and of the Order of Saint Francis—
having heard of my labor in explaining
such abstruse marks, brought me a certain script.
It was carved into a rock on Mount Sinai in letters a
span and a half <note>original: *sesquipalmaribus*; a "palm" was a traditional unit of measurement, making these letters roughly 10–12 inches tall</note>
high. This script had been recorded by the Reverend Father Thomas Obecinus
of Novara <note>Tommaso Obicini (1585–1632), an influential Franciscan orientalist and linguist</note>, of the same Franciscan Family,
a man widely known everywhere for his
outstanding erudition and skill in Oriental languages.
While he was formerly traveling through those regions,
he copied it with his own hands with the greatest
diligence and faithfulness, and brought it with him to
Rome with the intention of proposing it to Europeans
as a kind of hieroglyphic puzzle,
by the investigation of which they might test the powers
of their intellect. For I hear that this unique script
has so far so tormented the minds of scholars of the East
that there have even been those
who claimed it was completely impossible to explain; Some

...on account of the difficulty, some counted it among hieroglyphics; others among <term>Cabalistic</term> <note>Referring to the Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism often involving the interpretation of secret meanings in letters and numbers</note> symbols; others, finally, invented other things about it, as usually happens in such arduous and abstruse matters.

Therefore, when I had more deeply inspected this script—which in the opinion of all Easterners was inexplicable—having first been offered to me by the disposal of God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: *D.O.M.*, an abbreviation for *Deo Optimo Maximo*</note>, soon there came to mind that **Apuleian** script <note>Kircher refers to a passage in Apuleius's *The Golden Ass* (Metamorphoses) describing secret books written in mysterious, knotted characters</note> brought forth from the inner sanctuaries, marked with unrecognizable letters, partly knotted and twisted in the manner of a wheel, and partly marked with peaks crowded together like vine-tendrils. However, I was so far from losing heart because of these things, or despairing of penetrating the script, that I held nothing more important—my mind being invaded by an unusual desire to know the truth—than to test all my industry and the powers of my intellect in investigating and understanding the greatest mysteries which, by I know not what instinct, I recognized to lie beneath it. 

Therefore, having first implored Divine aid, I soon began a diligent comparison using the three languages—**Hebrew**, **Samaritan**, and **Syriac**—to which the characters of the said script seemed most closely to approach; I also applied my usual rules of the <term>art of combinations</term> <note>original: *artis combinatoriæ*; a method Kircher used to find patterns and hidden meanings through the systematic rearrangement of symbols</note>. And behold! The meaning of a script otherwise most intricate and, in the opinion of all, inexplicable, was made clear and unlocked for everyone—sooner than expected and with no great or singular labor (to God the Father of Lights be the honor).

## The authentic testimony of Father Tommaso Obicini of Novara regarding this writing.

<note>Tommaso Obicini (1585–1632) was a Franciscan friar, a pioneering orientalist, and a linguist who served in the Middle East. Kircher relies on his first-hand accounts to validate the existence of these inscriptions.</note>

These figures or letters are found carved into a small stone located at the foot of Mount Horeb <note>original Latin/Italian: "Monte Oreb," another name for Mount Sinai</note>, where God Our Lord gave the Law; one can see that the stone is part of the very root of the mountain. However, it is only slightly elevated from the ground. The Fathers <note>the monks of Saint Catherine’s Monastery</note> and the Arabs who accompanied me told me that there was a tradition among them that this writing was the work of the Prophet Jeremiah. They said, however, that no one had ever been able to interpret it; because of this, they believed that Jeremiah was revealing through those letters the place where he had hidden the sacred vessels of the Temple. 

Those Fathers further affirmed to me that some devout monks from the monastery (which is nearby) frequently testify to having seen a wondrous splendor shining above that stone. As for the historical fact of Jeremiah hiding the sacred vessels, we find this in the book of Maccabees, in the second chapter of the second book <note>referring to 2 Maccabees 2:4-8, which describes Jeremiah hiding the Tabernacle and the Ark in a cave</note>; however, it does not say there that he ascended Mount Horeb, but rather the mountain which Moses ascended to see the inheritance of God—and this was Mount Nebo, located in the land of Moab, opposite Jericho, as we read in Deuteronomy 34. 

Be that as it may, I wished to record this for the exercise of the virtuous <note>Kircher often uses "virtuosi" to refer to the learned or scholarly community</note>. It should be noted that as the writing is carved into the "spine" or ridge of the stone, some of the letters lean toward one side and some toward the other. They are more than a palm and a half in size <note>a "palm" was a traditional unit of measurement; a palm and a half would be roughly 12 to 14 inches</note>; and those holes that are shown...

For just as the four-letter name of God, the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>original: Τεραγραμματον</note>, according to the testimony of <term>Rabbi Hakkadosh</term> <note>Rabbi Judah the Prince, a famous 2nd-century scholar</note>, denotes God as the one who generates, and consequently as a Trinity: in such a way that through the <term>Yod</term> <note>י</note> is meant the principle or the first person, the Father; through the <term>He</term> <note>ה</note>, the Son, the second person; and through the <term>Vau</term> <note>ו</note>, finally, the connection, or bond, or love—namely the Holy Spirit. However, through the two <term>Hes</term> <note>ה</note>, a double aspect of the second person is designated: namely, as the one produced and the one producing, or even the two <note>original: δυσς</note> natures in Christ. Thus, I say, it is likely that this writer indicated the three divine persons, or co-eternal and consubstantial <term>hypostases</term> <note>a theological term for the distinct persons of the Trinity</note>, through these three <term>apices</term> <note>calligraphic strokes or "points"; see diagram</note>, each of which enjoys a circle. 

The Father is indicated by the first; the Son by the second (which, being in the middle, consists of two circles not without reason, so that the double aspect in the second person mentioned just before, or the two <note>original: δυσς</note> natures in Christ—namely the divine and the human—might be designated). Finally, by the third stroke, he indicated the Holy Spirit. Certainly, <term>Galatinus</term> <note>Pietro Galatino, an Italian monk and scholar of the Kabbalah</note> demonstrates these sayings so clearly that he seems to have taken up my own role in explaining this name. For in Book 2, Chapter 10, pages 49 and 50, he discusses it thus: *“The letters of the name of God, the Tetragrammaton, are four in number, which is why it is called the Tetragrammaton. # Final Chapter: Coptic Letters among Hieroglyphs #

Regarding this subject matter—as it is difficult, unknown, and treated by no one, and thus rare, sterile, and unproductive—I shall attempt to temper the boredom arising in the reader with this reasoning. It is, perhaps, not unwelcome, serving as a final course <note>original: "vltimo missu"; continuing the banquet metaphor from the previous page where he compares his book to a meal</note>, and one which (unless my opinion deceives me) is by no means flavorless.

The question is asked: were the ancient Egyptian <term>Hieromantæ</term> <note>Sacred interpreters or priests, from the Greek "hieros" (sacred) and "mantes" (prophet)</note> accustomed to insert the characters and names of the common language into hieroglyphic marks? I hesitate; for I find no one among the classic authors who has handed down anything regarding this proposed question, as most were of the opinion that the ancient Egyptians possessed no other letters at all besides the sacred ones. This is in accordance with that passage from Lucan, Book 3:

-> *Memphis had not yet learned to weave the river-papyrus,* <-
-> *And only upon stones did it preserve birds, wild beasts,* <-
-> *And carved animals as magical languages.* <-
<note>This quote from the Roman poet Lucan's "Pharsalia" suggests that before the invention of papyrus, Egyptians only wrote using animal symbols on stone.</note>

Indeed, I judge that this erroneous opinion arose from the fact that they were ignorant of which vernacular the ancient Egyptians used, what common method of writing they possessed, and finally, what difference existed between the common and the sacred characters. 

However, having applied an exact scrutiny to the said difficulty, and through frequent comparison of individual characters with one another, weighing the matter a little more scrupulously, we have found that the situation is much different. Nevertheless, so that something certain may be established regarding an argument so new, unusual, and <term>paradoxical</term> <note>original: παράδοξον (paradoxon); something contrary to common belief or expectation</note>, and so that the truth of our opinion may shine forth more clearly...

# Chapter 6: Coptic Letters among Hieroglyphs #

<page-num>221</page-num>

To demonstrate more clearly regarding the letters and scripts of the ancient Egyptians, it seemed appropriate to present briefly, and only according to the views of others, a preliminary taste of the subject. <margin>Among the Egyptians there are three types of letters.</margin> Note, therefore, that three types of characters were commonly used among the Egyptians: namely, <term>Epistolographic</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπιστολογραφικήν; literally "letter-writing" or "correspondence" script</note>, <term>Hieratic</term> <note>original Greek: ἱερατικήν; "priestly" script</note>, and <term>Hieroglyphic</term> <note>original Greek: ἱερογλυφικήν; "sacred carvings"</note>. Clement of Alexandria writes about these in Book 5 of the *Stromata* <note>The "Stromata" or "Miscellanies" is a major work by the 2nd-century Christian theologian Clement of Alexandria, providing one of the few ancient descriptions of Egyptian writing</note> in these words:

<note>original Greek: Αὐτίκα οἱ παρ’ Αἰγυπτίοις παιδευόμενοι πρῶτον μὲν πάντων τὴν Αἰγυπτίων γραμμάτων μέθοδον ἐκμανθάνουσιν...</note> 
"Those who are educated among the Egyptians learn, first of all, the method of Egyptian letters called Epistolographic; second, the Hieratic, which the sacred scribes use; and lastly and finally, the Hieroglyphic. Of the Hieroglyphic, one kind is <term>kyriologic</term> <note>meaning "proper" or "literal," using the primary elements or letters of the alphabet</note> through the first elements, while the other is symbolic. Of the symbolic kind, one is kyriologic by imitation <note>where the image directly represents the object</note>; another is written as if <term>tropically</term> <note>metaphorically or figuratively</note>; and another is directly allegorical according to certain enigmas. For instance, when they want to write 'Sun', they make a circle; for 'Moon', they make a crescent shape," etc.

*Those who are instructed by the Egyptians learn, first of all,* <margin>Epistolographic</margin> *that way and method of Egyptian letters which they call <term>Epistolographic</term>.* *That is to say, the script which they used everywhere at that time—as it was common to all of Egypt—for writing letters in the common language.* <margin>The epistolary script was none other than Coptic.</margin> *It will become clear from what follows that this was indeed none other than Coptic.* 

*The second is the <term>Hieratic</term> or Sacerdotal script, used by the <term>sacred scribes</term>* <note>original: "οἱ ἱερογραμματεῖς"</note>, *namely those who write about sacred matters.* <margin>Hieratic or Sacerdotal.</margin> *That is, those who recorded the hidden mysteries of their theology or philosophy in a certain secret system of characters, fashioned from various forms and similarities of natural things and figures of artificial things, established by the wise men of Egypt...*

the "running hieroglyphic character." Indeed, it does not seem to differ from hieroglyphs except that the former was proper to the <term>Sacred Scribes</term> <note>original Greek: τῶν ἱερογραμματίων (tōn hierogrammatiōn)</note>, whose duty it was to express those things that they could not paint (due to a lack of artistic skill or space) in a smaller character better suited for writing. The latter, however, belonged to the <term>Hieroglyph-carvers</term> <note>original Greek: τῶν ἱερογλύφων (tōn hieroglyphōn)</note>, whose task was to carve the larger sacred diagrams of symbols into rocks and stones according to the rules of the art of sculpture. 

However, there are some who assert that this "Priestly script" was composed of the mystical figures of a certain alphabet, such as those which <note>Teseo Ambrogio (1469–1540) was an Italian scholar who wrote one of the first comprehensive studies of various Eastern languages</note> Ambrosius Theseus brings forward in the appendix of his *Introduction to Various Oriental Languages*. But since I find no traces of this alphabet among actual hieroglyphic monuments, I rightly judge that it should be counted among other forgeries. Even so, it is certain that the Egyptians possessed another certain mystical alphabet, besides the common letters (the strokes of which were not entirely lacking in mysteries), as is demonstrated abundantly in my <term>Oedipus</term> <note>Kircher is referring to his own encyclopedic work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, where he attempted to "solve" the riddle of the hieroglyphs</note>.

Finally, the last type of script is the <term>Hieroglyphic</term> <note>original Greek: ἱερογλυφικήν</note>, that is, the sacred carved script. One kind of this is <term>kyriologic</term> <note>original Greek: κυριολογική; meaning "literal" or "proper" use of language</note> through the first elements [of the alphabet]...

# Chapter the Last: Coptic Letters among the Hieroglyphs #

<page-num>223</page-num>

<margin>Cyriologic <note>original Greek: Κυριολογικη (Kyriologikē), meaning speaking literally or using words in their primary sense.</note></margin>
<margin>Tropical <note>original Greek: Τροπικη (Tropikē), meaning metaphorical or figurative.</note></margin>
that is, speaking properly [or literally]; or that which expresses a thing through similar characters. The other, however, is **symbolic**, that is, signifying through signs; and of the symbolic type, one speaks properly through **imitation**, another is written as if **tropically** [metaphorically], and another is taken openly **allegorically** through certain enigmas. For example, those who wish to write "Sun" make a circle. For the "Moon," they make a figure displaying the form of the Moon's horns, suited to that form which is called "proper" [literal]. The **Tropical** or metaphorical style is that which transfers the various forms and figures of different things—especially animals—to signify either the dignities and mysteries of the Gods, or of other things pertaining to divine worship. Thus, by means of the **Ibis** and the **Scarab-shaped Hawk**, they indicate hieroglyphically that the Moon participates in its beauty from the Sun—namely the light, which is a certain image of divine beauty and is hinted at by the Hawk; just as the Sun and Moon are represented by the Scarab and the Ibis.

With these things having been premised and, as it were, presupposed, I say that not only sacred characters, or those which they call <term>Cyriologic</term> <note>original Greek: κυριολογικούς (kyriologikous), referring to the direct representation of objects</note> or <term>Priestly</term> <note>original Greek: ἱερατικούς (hieratikous)</note>, are found in hieroglyphs; but characters and names of the common **Coptic language** are also inserted. This is a doctrine that to many before now was not only <term>paradoxical</term> <note>original Greek: παράδοξον (paradoxon), meaning contrary to expectation or "strange"</note>, but even to some—what is more—utterly <term>impossible</term> <note>original Greek: ἀδύνατον (adynaton)</note>. But let us clarify these statements with examples.

I think it is unknown to no one; that most famous hieroglyphic monument of antiquity...

Truly, since these are the initial letters of words, and accordingly reflect the specific mind and sense of those using them, it has not been possible until now to investigate what they might mean, as they are situated far beyond the limits of human knowledge. <margin>What the character of the cross means</margin>
Fifthly, from the center of the Lunar circle, a character is placed that is spread out in the likeness of a cross. By this, the movements of the **4 elements** <term>4 elementorum</term>—insofar as they are subject to the influences of the Sun and Moon—are expressed through a certain hidden likeness of nature. 

<margin>What Phylo means</margin>
Sixthly, a small tablet is displayed to be seen with an inscription of the word **Love** <note>original Greek: *Phylo*, likely a variation of *Philo*, meaning love or attraction.</note>. This indicates that these parts of the world cannot be preserved at all unless they are joined together by love, acting as a kind of glue for the whole universe. According to their opinion, since this love proceeds from nowhere else but the **Soul of the World** <term>anima mundi</term> (of which love is a particular affection), they therefore added a seventh symbol. 

<margin>What the winged globe means</margin>
This is the **winged globe** <term>globus alatus</term>, with snakes leaping out from its hollowed center on both sides. It is a symbol of the aforementioned Soul of the World, which permeates all things and brings them to life with vital heat. <margin>The Scarab signifies the world.</margin>
Firstly, therefore, regarding the symbol of the **Scarab** <term>Scarabæus</term> <note>The dung beetle, *Scarabaeus sacer*, which the ancients observed rolling balls of dung; they believed this mirrored the movement of the sun across the sky.</note>, Horapollo teaches in the clearest words (Book 1, Hieroglyphica 50) that it signified the world among the ancient Egyptians—in addition to the testimonies of **Eusebius Pamphilus**, **Manetho**, **Hecatæus** (quoted by **Diogenes Laertius**), and others.
<margin>Horapollo.</margin>

### Last Chapter: A Specimen of Hieroglyphic Interpretation ###

The reason that the head of Horus is joined to a Scarab <note>The dung beetle, which the Egyptians associated with the god Khepri and the self-generating power of the morning sun.</note> is so that by this <term>beetle-form</term> <note>original Greek: κανθαρομόρφωσιν (kantharomorphosin)</note> it might be suggested that the entire universe—which we said just a moment ago was signified by the Scarab—is governed by the providence and intellect of the Sun. For this reason, Plato <note>The Athenian philosopher (c. 427–347 BC). In his work "The Republic," he uses the Sun as an analogy for the Form of the Good, calling it the "offspring" of the Good.</note> did not say incongruously that the Sun was the "visible son of the invisible God." <note>original Latin: inuisibilis Dei visibilem filium</note>

<margin>Clement</margin>
And that this is indeed the case is easily proven from Clement of Alexandria <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 150–215 AD) who wrote extensively on the relationship between Greek philosophy, Egyptian "mysteries," and Christian truth.</note>, who in Book 5 of the *Stromata* <note>Meaning "Miscellanies," a work where Clement discusses a wide variety of topics, including Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, when discussing the composition of Egyptian Sphinxes, records that a human face joined to any other animal signified character and wisdom <note>original Latin: ingenium & prudentiam</note> to the ancients.

<margin>Porphyry</margin>
But these matters are demonstrated even more clearly in Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who frequently sought the hidden symbolic meanings within pagan religious practices.</note> in Book 4, page 76, of *On Abstinence from Animal Food*. "In the crafting of the Gods," he says, "every animal was assumed by the Egyptians alongside man; in this they mixed the bodies of cattle, man, and birds, and likewise man with others. For among them, individual statues of the Gods either display a human form right up to the neck, but have the face of a bird, a lion, or some other animal imposed upon it; or conversely, they show the body of another animal placed beneath a human head."

Therefore, according to the stated reasoning, the <term>beetle-formed</term> <note>original Greek: κανθαρομόρφον (kantharomorphon)</note> Horus is an open symbol of the Solar intelligence governing the world. This is shown above all by the type of gem found in Pignorius <note>Lorenzo Pignoria (1571–1631), an Italian scholar and antiquarian who published studies on Egyptian artifacts, notably the "Bembine Tablet" or Mensa Isiaca.</note>, in which the radiant head of the Sun or Horus is elegantly placed upon a Scarab, and a snake devouring its tail <note>The Ouroboros, an ancient symbol of eternity, the cycles of nature, and the unity of the cosmos.</note> surrounds it all; so that it might be understood that Horus, or the Sun, [is the ruler] of time and of yea—

The upward movement of love, indicated—and not without reason—by the radiant letter **V** <note>The author is likely referring to the Greek letter Upsilon ($\Upsilon$), which in Renaissance typography and symbolic study often resembled the Latin 'V'. *that it is a certain circle perpetually revolving from the good toward the good* <note>original: "ut quiddam sit circulus à bono in bonum perpetuò reuolutus"</note>; For, as it begins from God and entices, it displays the principle of perfect beauty; however, as it passes into the world, it is chiefly called "Love." Pleasure, finally, as it returns to its Author, transforms the beautiful image into its beautiful archetype by a beautiful revolution. In this circuit, penetrating through all things, it causes them to be continually rolled upward and downward with itself; not unlike a single ray of the Sun, uniform in itself, which creates light in Heaven, splendor in the ether, illumination in the elements, and bright color in mixed bodies. It is clear, therefore, that

<margin>The order of love is the cause of things.</margin>

the order of love is the cause of the return in all things toward divine beauty and the primary form, and (to use the words of Proclus <note>A 5th-century Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on how all things "revert" or return to their divine source.</note>) it leads back all subsequent things to it, joining them to it and confirming those already joined; and presently filling those that follow, it distributes the gifts of divine light springing from there through the whole universe. Moral philosophers <note>Original Latin: *Ethici*.</note>, however, would read it this way: The rational soul makes the whole man, including the higher powers—the intellect and the will—concordant with the lower and outer senses through the dictate of right reason; and so we leave the rest of the applications to be made by the Reader.

You see, therefore, how many things, and how profound, the Egyptians indicated with such ingenuity through this simple hieroglyphic diagram. You see how they have drawn all other things analogous to it, linked as if in a chain, toward one universal idea. Indeed, it is done in such a way that the meaning is not content with a single sense, but is extended through innumerable analogous types of things. By a certain hidden similarity, these symbols seem to have expressed the process and sequence of all things, even the very mysteries of the Christians.

<margin>Four spheres correspond to the 4 elements</margin>
Lest anyone think this four-fold system was invented by the Egyptians for no reason, I have decided that its mystery must be indicated here. The Egyptians, therefore, when they had grasped from that wonderful connection and concatenation of all things that the superior bodies move the inferior ones quite powerfully; and that the 4 elements are subjected to the 4 spheres as active principles; moreover, that an effective power exists in the Lunar sphere for moving the element of water, in the Solar sphere for fire, in the sphere of the 5 planets for air (on account of the various mixtures of their rays); and finally, in the <term>firmament</term> <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, believed to be the outermost visible shell of the universe.</note> itself for altering the earth; who does not see that they, with great genius, [constructed] this four-fold chain, the four-fold similarities of the inferior and superior world...

### Final Chapter: A Specimen of Hieroglyphic Interpretation

As with countless other things, which will be treated specifically in *Oedipus* <note>Referring to Kircher's massive work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, where he attempted to fully decode Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, furthermore, this present hieroglyphic figure was one whose magical powers, together with the rites and ceremonies they used in making such things, I would gladly present. However, since the enemy of the human race <note>A traditional term for the Devil.</note> is usually accustomed to secretly involve himself in operations of this kind, and many things concerning their making are encountered that are utterly contrary to Christian piety and long ago prohibited by Holy Mother Church, I will gladly suppress them now—as in other cases—lest I be a stumbling block to tender minds by reciting them, unless the good of the Church, which I serve, suggests otherwise; but I leave this to be judged by those to whom I am subject in this regard <note>Kircher is referring to his Jesuit superiors and the ecclesiastical censors.</note>.

You have, therefore, a hieroglyphic system that is truly most beautiful and entirely musical, which, joined by unequal intervals but nonetheless distinct according to a calculated proportion, tempering high sounds with low ones, produces various harmonies equally. This is true even if our ears do not catch it, as they are deafened by <term>sublunary</term> <note>The realm below the moon (Earth), characterized by change and decay, as opposed to the eternal heavens.</note> whirlwinds and various storms of the passions, just like those living at the <term>Cataracts of the Nile</term> <note>original: catadupa Nili. Ancient writers claimed the inhabitants near the Great Cataracts of the Nile became deaf from the constant roar of the water.</note>. You have all the secrets of philosophy in this single symbolic diagram, sketched out with a mysterious likeness of things as if in a certain compendium and <term>recapitulation</term> <note>original Greek: anakephalaiōsei (ἀνακεφαλαιώσει), meaning a summary or bringing together of parts under one head.</note> of the whole world. Indeed, I did not wish to show its entire glory to be seen immediately from the very entrance; both because its scope, and broadly...

-> # Chapter 5, Last Part: A Specimen of Hieroglyphic Interpretation <-

No one may easily survey this widespread domain unless he enters more deeply, or directs his mind even into its innermost sanctuaries. This is because its brilliance and unspeakable keenness so strike every nerve of the soul, and so exceed all power, strength, and abundance of speech, that no river of genius is so fertile, and no oration so studiously refined, that it could grasp either the appearance or the magnitude of such true praise. It is better, therefore, not to pursue this method of writing with far-fetched praises, but—as was customary in the mysteries of the Egyptians—to venerate it with silence alone, as one would a Divinity. We should be content with a somewhat rough image of its use, until **Silenus** <note>A reference to the "Sileni of Alcibiades," a classical metaphor for something that appears ugly or unremarkable on the outside but contains a beautiful, divine image within.</note> here reveals himself completely and drenches all things in a sudden ray of divinity. I add only this: whoever penetrates the Egyptian mind lying hidden under this sculpture will easily understand what that <term>mystical</term> <note>Referring to hidden, spiritual knowledge.</note> term <term>Hammekkabalim</term> <note>original: המקבלם, meaning "The Kabbalists" or "Those who receive the tradition."</note> intends to say.

He who knows the secret of the union of **Beauty** <note>original Hebrew: *Tipheret*, a sphere on the Kabbalistic Tree of Life representing harmony.</note> with **Kingdom** <note>original Hebrew: *Malkuth*, the sphere representing the physical world or the manifestation of God’s sovereignty.</note> through the foundation of the **Infinite** <note>original Hebrew: *Ein Sof*, the infinite Godhead prior to any self-manifestation.</note>, and the emergence of **Wisdom** <note>original Hebrew: *Chokhmah*.</note> from **Nothingness** <note>original Hebrew: *Me-ayin*, a concept in Kabbalah where divine wisdom emerges from a state of non-being.</note>, will succeed in my sayings and know the secret of the high mountains.

*He who knows how in the sephirotic tree <note>The Tree of Life in Kabbalah, composed of ten spheres or "Sephirot."</note> **Beauty** and **Kingdom** are joined through the **Infinite**, and how the emergence of **Wisdom** comes from **Nothingness**; he shall be enlightened by these words, and shall know the secrets of the highest mountains. He shall also know toward what end the enigmatic words of **Algazel** <note>The Latinized name for Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111), a famous Persian philosopher and theologian.</note>, the Arab Philosopher, in his book **On Influences**, are directed.*

### Final Chapter: A Specimen of Hieroglyphic Interpretation

Whoever knows the chain by which the higher world is joined to the lower knows the secrets of nature and performs miracles.
<note>original Arabic: كل من يعرف السلسله التي يلفق بها العالم العالي مع التحتي هو يعرف الاسرار الطبيعية فيفعل المعجزات</note>

Whoever knows that bond, or that great chain connecting the upper world to the lower, will know all the mysteries of nature and will act as a performer of wonders. For that is the source of all happiness derived from heaven to earth, which the Ethiopians call the **Celestial Nile**. From this comes that mystical proverb common among the Ethiopians:

<margin>Ethiopic saying.</margin>
The Nile is celestial; it is that which flows over your land, it shall fill it, and you shall be fed by its riches, and it shall grant you the request of your heart.
<note>original Ge'ez: ጕየን፡ ፈልገ፡ሰማያዊ፡ዘይፈስስ፡ውእቱ፡ፈልገ፡ወተመልክ፡መሬት፡በኩሉ፡ሠናይቲ፡ወይረዊከ፡ዲበ፡ብልስ፡ወይሁበከ፡ስእለተ፡ልብከ፡</note>

The Celestial Nile is that which, having been derived upon your earth, will fill it, and you shall feed upon its riches, and your desire shall be fulfilled. Beneath this, you will find clearly hidden that Egyptian mystery cited above:

<margin>Egyptian</margin>
**HEAVEN ABOVE, HEAVEN BELOW, STARS ABOVE, STARS BELOW, ALL THINGS ABOVE, ALL THINGS BELOW. UNDERSTAND THESE THINGS AND BE HAPPY.**
<note>original Greek: ΟΥΡΑΝΟ ΑΝΩ, ΟΥΡΑΝΟ ΚΑΘΩ, ΑCΤΡΑ ΑΝΩ, ΑCΤΡΑ ΚΑΘΩ, ΠΑΝΤΑ ΑΝΩ, ΠΑΝΤΑ ΚΑΘΩ. ΤΑΥΤΑ ΚΑΤΑΛΑΒΕ ΚΕ ΕΥΤΥXHC. This is a famous Hermetic axiom similar to the "As above, so below" of the Emerald Tablet.</note>

Beneath this, you will uncover that wonderful fountain, of which one reads thus in the **Oracles of the Ancient Chaldeans**:
<note>The Chaldean Oracles were a collection of mystical poems from the 2nd century AD, highly prized by Neoplatonists and Renaissance mages like Kircher.</note>

<margin>Chaldean Oracle.</margin>
They say there is also an archetypal sun from the material source, and an archangelic source, and a source of sensation, and a source of judgment, and a lightning-filled source, and a source falling from Zeus, and a formative source presiding over the unknown tokens, and the source-summits of Apollo, and Osiris, and Hermes.
<note>original Greek: φασὶ δὲ καὶ ἀρχικὸν ἥλιον ἀπὸ τῆς ὑλικῆς πηγῆς, καὶ ἀρχαγγελικὸν καὶ πηγὴν αἰθήσιος, καὶ πηγαιάν κρίσιν, καὶ κεραύνιον πηγήν, καὶ πηγὴν διοπετῆ, καὶ χαρακτήριον πηγὴν ἐπιβατεύσαν τοῖς ἀγνώστοις συνθήμασι, καὶ πηγαίας ἀκρότητας Ἀπόλλωνος καὶ Ὁσίሪδος καὶ Ἑρμοῦ.</note>

<margin>
The Assembly of the Philosophers
<note>original: Turba Philosophorum. This refers to a famous early Latin alchemical text, though Kircher uses it here to refer to a broader group of ancient mystical thinkers.</note>

They <note>the ancient sages</note> place the *Sun* as the commander, the fountain of mirrors, the source of characters, presiding over unknown signs and symbols, and the fountain-like summits of *Apollo*, *Osiris*, and *Mercury*. From this it will finally be clearly evident to the wise mind how the **Love of the World** <note>original: Amor mundi. Kircher refers here to the Neoplatonic concept of a cosmic binding force or World-Soul that unites all things.</note> is the most excellent metaphysician, physicist, astrologer, musician, geometer, arithmetician, dialectician, rhetorician, poet, historiographer, legal expert, ethicist, physician, sailor, farmer, architect, painter, hunter, gardener, augur, and <term>universal seer</term> <note>original: Παντομάντις (Pantomantis)</note>; in a word, the most perfect <term>Magus</term> <note>meaning a master of natural philosophy and divine secrets.</note>. But I finish in good time, lest having entered this immense ocean of vastness, I find I cannot withdraw my foot. And these are the things, Kind Reader, which I wanted to inform you of through this my *Prodromus* <note>meaning "Precursor" or "Forerunner." This book was intended as an introduction to his later work.</note> regarding both the common and the hieroglyphic language of the Egyptians, before I gave light to the *Thesaurus of the Coptic Language* and after that the *Egyptian Oedipus*. I wished to send it forth here so that you might approach the works to follow more readily and with greater pleasure, and at the same time might become better instructed to understand them through these prerequisites. However, as far as the method of this *Prodromus* is concerned, I confess that I have passed over many things here which, since they required a long and exact explanation, would be more conveniently...

...we have referred back to our *Oedipus* <note>Kircher refers to his forthcoming masterwork, "Oedipus Aegyptiacus," where he intended to fully "solve" the riddle of the hieroglyphs.</note>; I too have omitted many of those things for which certain knowledge could not be obtained, or have perhaps too often repeated obscure points, as the great complexity of the subjects and the difficulty of the matters to be handled requires. ->*Second thoughts are wiser.* <note>original: δ’ ἕτεραι φροντίδες σοφώτεραι (d’ heterai phrontides sophoterai)</note><-

In the meantime, kind and honest Reader, if you possess any hieroglyphic monuments of antiquity; if you have books on this subject, or Gems, Mummies, <term>Canopic jars</term> <note>Egyptian jars used to hold the internal organs of the deceased; Kircher viewed their decorations as symbolic keys.</note>, Idols, or any other items in which symbols of this kind—smelling of Egypt—are seen depicted; out of the care you feel for promoting the good of the <term>Republic of Letters</term> <note>original: Reip[ublicae] Lit[terariae]. <margin>||</margin>->**Whoever adds, to him it shall be added; and whoever subtracts, from him it shall be subtracted.** <note>original: כל המוסיף מוסיפין לו והגורע גורעין לו (Kol ha-mosif mosifin lo ve-ha-gore'a gor'in lo)</note><-

*To the one who adds, it shall be added; and from the one who subtracts, it shall be subtracted.*
*For the doors of the Muses are free from envy.* <note>original: Ἄφθονοι γὰρ Μουσῶν θύραι (Aphthonoi gar Mouson thyrai)</note> *Indeed, it shall be so that just as you are a partner in my labor, so too shall you be a sharer in the fruit. I, truly relying upon your assistance, may truly say:*
<sig>n 4</sig>*For the time being, we have made you in marble; but if the*
*full flock fills the fold, you shall be of gold.* <note>original: "Nunc te marmoreū pro tempore fecimus; at tu si satura gregem suppleuerit, aureus esto." A modified quote from Virgil’s Eclogues, suggesting this book is a modest "marble" start, but the future work will be "golden."</note>

## Note.

Since there were several blank pages left at this point after the completion of the *Prodromus* <note>original: "Prodromo"; refers to this current book, the "Coptic Precursor."</note>, I thought it would be worthwhile if, for the sake of those who take pleasure in the <term>study of various scripts</term> <note>original: "characterum studio." In the 17th century, the study of "characters" referred to the deciphering of ancient or foreign writing systems.</note>, I were to also subjoin the alphabets of those languages which this precursor has brought forward to confirm the matters asserted; so that I might not seem to have omitted anything that could be for the convenience or benefit of a lover of letters.

## *To the Most Eminent Prince of the Holy Roman Church, Cardinal:*
## FRANCESCO BARBERINI. <note>Francesco Barberini (1597–1679) was a powerful cardinal and patron of the arts and sciences, and the nephew of Pope Urban VIII. He was a central figure in the intellectual life of 17th-century Rome.</note>

### *Preface.*

**S**ince it is so arranged for us by nature, Most Eminent Prince, that we do not fully rest regarding those things which we either admire for their novelty or which we are held by a burning desire to learn, until we receive a full and entire instruction concerning them; we daily experience this to be the case in all things, but most especially in matters pertaining to <term>science</term> <note>Latin: *scientiam*; in this context, it refers to systematic knowledge or scholarship.</note>. Certainly, I thought I would perform a task by no means ungrateful to eager and curious readers if—now that the *Prodromus* <note>Referring to Kircher's 1636 work *Prodromus Coptus siue Aegyptiacus* (The Coptic or Egyptian Precursor), which was his first major publication on the language.</note> has been dispatched, in which I discussed the properties of the Coptic language only in general terms—I were to also subjoin in this place a certain special, brief, and clear treatment regarding the precepts and rules of this language. I do this so that I might not seem to have omitted anything in our *Prodromus* necessary for fully understanding Coptic matters. Therefore, having examined without delay a great quantity indeed of Coptic Grammars, which partly the— <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page.</note>

# Preface

*...<term>Coptic-Arabic Thesaurus</term> <note>Latin: *Thesauro Coptarabico*; referring to a bilingual dictionary or collection of texts Kircher compiled or used as a primary source.</note>, and partly those I found prefixed as a collection to other **Vatican Codices**; I have undertaken to compile this present summary, which, according to the accustomed laws of our Grammarians, I have freed from all confusion and arranged with such a method that whatever was either obscure in the **Arabic version**, or difficult because of a foreign method of teaching, might be delivered here briefly, clearly, and lucidly, adapted to the minds of **beginners** <note>Latin: *Tyronum*; literally 'recruits' or 'novices' in the study of the language.</note>. Lest the reader perhaps, because of the thorny traditions of an unknown language, should cast aside the desire to learn them out of weariness, I have reserved the treatment of more minute matters or certain particles having more difficulty for the **Coptic Thesaurus** <note>Referring to Kircher’s larger project, the *Lingua Aegyptiaca Restituta* (1643), which he intended as a more exhaustive reference.</note>, in which the reader will find all those things pertaining to the perfect understanding of that language, treated more fully and deeply in **Coptic-Arabic-Latin**. Farewell, therefore, most munificent Prince, and in the meantime enjoy these few little things.*

# CHAPTER SECOND.
## On the pronunciation of certain letters.

**B**, Vida. As a consonantal "v," it is pronounced like the Greek beta <note>original: "β"</note>: as in **ⲃⲏⲑⲁⲛⲓⲁ** <note>original: "ⲃⲏⲑⲁⲛⲓⲁ"</note>. Vithania. Bethania. <note>In later Greek and Coptic, the letter "B" shifted from a hard "b" sound to a "v" sound, a phenomenon the author is highlighting here.</note>

**H**, Hida is similar to the Greek letter eta <note>original: "η"</note>, which is a long "I": it is pronounced like an "I" leaning toward an "E"; but when it is found with an accent above it **ⲓ̄**, 

<meta>catchword: pro- (likely "pronunciatur," meaning "it is pronounced")</meta>

it is pronounced as a clear I. An example of the former is **ⲏⲧⲉ**, pronounced almost like <gloss>äre</gloss> <note>The author uses "äre" to suggest a sound between 'a' and 'e'.</note>; and **ⲏⲓⲙⲓⲛ**, pronounced as *imin*.

**ⲛⲛ**, **Ni**. At the end of a word, it changes its shape and is written thus: <note>Final form of Coptic Ni, resembling a long j or l</note>, just like the Hebrew letter **Nun** <note>original: "נ"</note> when written in its final form **Nun Sophit** <note>original: "ן"</note>.
Examples: **ⲡⲣⲉⲧⲟⲩⲣⲓⲟⲛ** <note>Pretorion</note> and **ⲡⲓⲕⲩⲕⲗⲟⲛ** <note>Pikyklon</note>.

**ⲑ**, **Thida**, like the Greek letter **Theta** <note>original: "θ"</note>. For example: **ⲑⲱⲟⲩⲧ**, **Thoth**, which is the first month of the Egyptians.

**ⲡ**, **Bi**, is pronounced like a P. For example: **ⲡⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓ**, *piromi* <note>Coptic for "the man."</note>.

**ⲧ**, **Dau**. Although it is written as a T, it is nevertheless pronounced as a D.
Example: **ⲧⲉⲧⲉⲛⲛⲁϩϯ**, *tetennahdi*, meaning <gloss>he believed</gloss>.

**ⲩ**, **He** <note>The letter Upsilon.</note>. It is sometimes pronounced like an I or a Y, and after the letter **ⲁ** it functions as the vowel V. Examples: **ⲑⲩⲃⲓ**, *Thybi* <note>another Egyptian month</note>; and **ⲉⲧⲓⲙⲁⲩ**, *etimau*.

**ⲫ**, **Phi**. Sometimes it is a P, leaning toward a B sound. Example: **ⲫⲏⲗⲓⲝ**, *Philix* or *Bilix* <note>The author refers to the name Felix, showing the phonetic fluidness between P, F, and B.</note>.

**ⲭ**, **Chi**. This is pronounced without aspiration, in almost the same way the French usually pronounce the Greek <term>chi</term> <note>original: "χ"</note>.

**ⲯ**, **Ebsi**, is pronounced like the Greek letter <term>psi</term> <note>original: "ψ"</note>. Example: **ⲯⲩⲭⲏ**, *psychi* <note>meaning "soul."</note>.

**ϣ**, **Scei**, pronounced as "Sh," like the Hebrew letter **Shin** <note>original: "ש"</note> and the Arabic letter **Shin** <note>original: "ش"</note>. Example: **ⲛⲁⲩϣⲟⲡ**, *Naufschop*.

**ϧ**, **Ch** <note>The letter Chei.</note>. This is pronounced with aspiration, like the Hebrew letter **Het** <note>original: "ח"</note> or the Arabic letter **Kha** <note>original: "خ"</note>. For example: **ϧⲉⲛ**, *hhen*.

**ϩ**, **Hori**, an H sound, like the Hebrew letter **He** <note>original: "ה"</note> or the Arabic letter **Ha** <note>original: "ه"</note>.

# CHAPTER FOUR.

# PART II.
## On the Noun.

In Coptic nouns, five things must be considered: Quality, Species, Gender, Number, and Case, which must be dealt with briefly in as many chapters.

## CHAPTER II.

### On the Type of Nouns.

The "species" <note>In historical grammar, "species" refers to whether a word is a primary root or a derivative form.</note> among the Copts is twofold: Primitive and Derivative. A primitive noun is one that is not derived from another word, such as:

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| **The Heaven** <note>original: Ϯⲫⲉ</note> | Heaven | **Angel** <note>original: Ⲁⲅⲅⲉⲗⲟⲥ</note> | Angel. |

A derivative, however, is that which is derived from another word; it is either verbal or nominal. A verbal noun is one derived from a verb, which includes almost all adjectives and participles: such as <term>ⲉⲓϣⲁϫⲓ</term> (speaking) and others that are formed from a verb. A nominal noun, on the other hand, is one that draws its origin from a noun; such are all those adjectives formed from some common noun. For example:

|----------|----------------|--------------------------|
| **Spiritual** <note>original: Ⲡⲛⲁⲧⲓⲕⲟⲛ</note> | are derived from | **( Spirit** <note>original: Ⲡⲛⲁ</note> |

Of all these aforementioned articles, this one is the most common and frequent.

### Rule 3.

Every word which has the sign **ou** <note>original Coptic: ⲟⲩ</note> prefixed at the beginning signifies either a feminine or masculine noun indeterminately, without a <term>definite article; a word like "the" that points to a specific item. Here, it functions like "a" or "an"</term>.

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A man** <note>original: ⲟⲩⲣⲱⲙⲉ</note> | Man. | **A house** <note>original: ⲟⲩⲏⲓ</note> | House |
| **A woman** <note>original: ⲟⲩⲥϩⲓⲙⲉ</note> | Woman. | **A brother** <note>original: ⲟⲩⲥⲟⲛ</note> | Brother. |
| **A father** <note>original: ⲟⲩⲓⲱⲧ</note> | Father. | **A mother** <note>original: ⲟⲩⲙⲁⲁⲩ</note> | Mother. |

However, how this particle is specifically distinguished <note>referring to how one tells if the "ou" prefix refers to a masculine or feminine noun</note>, we have discussed above in the Arabic lesson <note>The author is likely referring to a previous section where Coptic grammar is explained through the lens of Arabic, which was the primary language of the Coptic community at the time of this manuscript's writing</note>.

## CHAPTER IV.

### *On the Number of Egyptian Nouns*

The numbers <term>grammatical categories expressing quantity</term> of nouns among the Copts are three: Singular, dual, and plural. We have already spoken of the singular and its meaning in the preceding sections; for the dual and plural, take the following rules.

#### Rule 1. 
Every noun of the plural number with a definite meaning <note>referring to "the" plural rather than "some" plural</note>, whether it be masculine or feminine, is designated by these prefixed articles:

->**Ni . Ne . Na . N .**<-
<note>These are the variations of the Coptic plural definite article "the".</note>

#### Rule 2. 
Every <term>indefinite noun; a noun referring to a non-specific person or thing, like "a dog" rather than "the dog"</term> of the plural number, whether it be of the masculine or feminine gender, is designated by the prefixed article **han** <note>original Coptic: ϩⲁⲛ</note>.

| Singular | | Plural | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| A man <note>original Coptic: ⲟⲩⲣⲱⲙⲉ</note> | man. | Some men <note>original Coptic: ϩⲁⲛⲣⲱⲙⲉ</note> | men. |
| A woman <note>original Coptic: ⲟⲩⲥϩⲓⲙⲓ</note> | woman. | Some women <note>original Coptic: ϩⲁⲛⲥϩⲓⲙⲓ</note> | women. |
| A mother <note>original Coptic: ⲟⲩⲙⲁⲩ</note> | mother. | Some mothers <note>original Coptic: ϩⲁⲛⲙⲁⲩ</note> | mothers. |
| The Angel <note>original Coptic: ⲡⲁⲅⲅⲉⲗⲟⲥ</note> | Angel. | Some Angels <note>original Coptic: ϩⲁⲛⲁⲅⲅⲉⲗⲟⲥ</note> | Angels. |

From these examples, it is evident that the Coptic language, in the <term>inflection; the way a word changes its form to show its grammatical role</term> of nouns, has no commonality with Greek. For among the Greeks, the plural is recognized by the ending of the noun; it is otherwise among the Copts, with whom the substance of the noun itself always remains intact, with the only change being made by the addition of the aforementioned particles <note>In other words, while Greek words change their endings to become plural, Coptic words usually stay the same and just change the "the" or "a" in front of them</note>.

#### Rule 3. 
Every noun, whether it be masculine or feminine, whose beginning is marked by the article **han** <note>original: ϩⲁⲛ</note> or **ni** <note>original: ⲛⲓ</note> and whose end is marked by the letter **b** <note>original: ⲃ</note>, which signifies "two" for the Copts, is of the <term>dual; a grammatical category used to describe exactly two of something</term> number. For example:

| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| A man <note>original Coptic: ⲟⲩⲣⲱⲙⲉ</note> | Men. <note>The original Latin manuscript labels the singular Coptic word as "viri" (men), though it is technically singular</note> | Two men <note>original Coptic: ϩⲁⲛⲣⲱⲙⲉⲃ</note> | two Men. |

## CHAPTER V.

### On the Case of Nouns.

Just as among the Hebrews, Chaldeans, Arabs, and Ethiopians <note>The author is comparing Coptic to other Semitic and Afroasiatic languages known to scholars at the time</note>, the <term>cases; the grammatical roles of a word like subject or object</term> are established by certain articles prefixed to nouns; so it is also among the Copts, although not as much account is taken of them as in Western languages <note>such as Latin or Greek, which use word endings rather than prefixes for case</note>. This is because the <term>affixes; additions to the beginning or end of words</term> can easily supply almost all their deficiency.

# Chapter 5: On the Case of Nouns

Having discussed those particles which serve the nominative cases in both the singular and the plural or dual, I find that other particles are also used indiscriminately for the remaining cases among the Copts. They are the following:

->**ⲛ̀ⲧⲉ. ⲛ̀. ⲛ̀ⲉ.**<-

**ⲛ̀ⲧⲉ.** <note>pronounced 'ente'</note> is a particle of the genitive <note>The genitive case indicates possession, like "of" in English.</note>. It is most especially suited to a noun that is in <term>regimine</term> <note>Latin for "government" or "construction"; this refers to a noun that is grammatically linked to another to show possession.</note>. This is clear in the following examples:

| | |
|:---|:---|
| **ⲛⲓⲫⲏⲟⲩⲓ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲛⲓⲫⲏⲟⲩⲓ** | The Heavens of the Heavens. |
| **ⲑⲙⲁⲩ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲫϯ** | The Mother of God. |
| **ⲟⲩϩⲟ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲡⲓⲕⲁϩⲓ** | A face of the earth. |
| **ⲛⲓⲟⲩⲣⲱⲟⲩ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲡⲓⲕⲁϩⲓ** | The Kings of the earth. |
| **ⲉ̀ⲃⲟⲗϩⲉⲛⲛⲓϫⲓϫ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲛⲉⲛϫⲁϫⲓ** | From the hands of our enemies. |
| **ⲡⲟⲩⲧⲁϩ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲧⲉⲛⲉϫⲓ** | The fruit of your womb. |
| **ⲫⲛⲟϩⲉⲙ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲧⲉⲕⲟⲩⲓⲛⲁⲙ** | The salvation of your right hand. |
| **ⲫⲟⲩⲱⲓⲛⲓ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲛⲁⲃⲁⲗ** | The light of my eyes. |
| **ⲧⲭⲁⲙⲉ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲧⲁϩⲉⲗⲡⲓⲥ** | The power <note>original: virtus</note> of my hope. |

However, I also often find the other particles **ⲛ̀.** <note>n</note> and **ⲛ̀ⲉ.** <note>ne</note> prefixed to the genitive. For example:

| | |
|:---|:---|
| **ⲡⲓⲥⲱⲙⲁ ⲙ̀ⲡⲟⲥ** | The Body of the Lord. |
| **ⲫⲩⲗⲏ ⲛ̀ⲓⲟⲩⲇⲁ** | The tribe of Judah. |
| **ⲫⲉⲛⲓⲛⲓ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲡⲉⲕϫⲓⲛⲓ** | The sign of your coming. |

Nevertheless, these particles for the most part serve the dative <note>The dative case usually indicates the indirect object, like "to" or "for".</note> and accusative <note>The accusative case indicates the direct object of a verb.</note> cases indiscriminately.

->The following are examples in the dative case:<-

However, as for when these two <term>particles</term> <note>small grammatical markers</note> **ǹ** and **`ε** serve the <term>Dative</term>, <term>Accusative</term>, or <term>Genitive</term>, or what the rules are for recognizing them—since they require a more extensive treatment—we have deferred speaking of them until our *Thesaurus* <note>Kircher refers here to a more comprehensive dictionary or grammatical "treasury" he intended to publish.</note>; for there, God willing, we shall explain the rules for each of these particles more fully. Therefore, we refer the reader to that work.

Furthermore, the <term>Vocative</term> <note>the case used for direct address, like calling someone's name</note> and <term>Ablative</term> <note>the case usually indicating movement "away from" or "by means of"</note> also claim their own specific prefixes. The Vocative indeed uses **O**, **o**, **ō**, and **che**, as in: **sotem pa laos**, "Hear, O my people"; **ō ti shimi**, "O woman"; **p choys**, "Lord," or **che p choys**, "O Lord."

# Chapter 5: On the Classification of Nouns. <note>The Latin heading "De genere Nominum" literally means "On the Gender of Nouns," but the text continues to discuss grammatical cases. This may be a heading error in the original manuscript or a broader use of "genus" to mean "type" or "nature."</note>

Although the Copts do not have an <term>Ablative</term> <note>In Latin grammar, the ablative case is used to show movement away from, location, or the instrument used in an action. Coptic lacks a specific noun ending for this, instead using prefixes.</note> case, they nevertheless express it through the attached <term>particles</term> <note>short words or prefixes that modify the meaning of a noun</note> **ϦEN, ϦEN, EBOL, EBOLϦEN.** That is: *of, in, from, or by*, just as is commonly done in other languages.

## Paradigm of Declension.

### Singular Number:

| <term>Case</term> | In Coptic | In English |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Nom: | **ⲡⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓ** | The Man. |
| Gen: | **ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲡⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓ** | Of the Man. |
| Dat: | **ⲉ̀ⲡⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓ** | To the Man. |
| Accus: | **ⲙ̀ⲡⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓ** | The Man <note>as a direct object</note>. |
| Voc: | **ⲱⲡⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓ** | O Man! |

For the Ablative, they place **EBOL, EBOLϦEN, or ϦEN** before the noun, as in: **EBOLⲡⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓ, EBOLϦENⲡⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓ, or ϦENⲡⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓ** [meaning] *from the Man.*

### Plural Number:

| <term>Case</term> | In Coptic | In English |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Nom: | **ⲛⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓ** | The Men. |
| Gen: | **ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲛⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓ** | Of the Men. |
| Dat: | **ⲉ̀ⲛⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓ** | To the Men. |
| Accus: | **ⲙ̀ⲛⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓ** | The Men <note>as a direct object</note>. |
| Vocat: | **ⲱⲛⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓ** | O Men! |

In place of the Ablative, they place **EBOL ϦEN** before the noun.

# PART III.
## On the Pronoun.

Pronouns take the place of a noun; they are either separate words or are <term>affixed</term> <note>attached as prefixes or suffixes</note> to other words. Separate pronouns are of three types: Personal, Demonstrative, and Relative, which vary by gender and number.

## CHAPTER I.
### On the Personal Pronoun.

| | 1st Person | 2nd Person | 3rd Person |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Singular:** | I <note>original Coptic: ⲁⲛⲟⲕ; Latin: ego</note> <note>common gender</note> | You <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲧⲟⲕ; Latin: tu</note> (masc.)<br>You <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲧⲟ; Latin: tu</note> (fem.) | He <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲧⲟϥ; Latin: ille</note> (masc.)<br>She <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲧⲟⲥ; Latin: illa</note> (fem.) |
| **Plural:** | We <note>original Coptic: ⲁⲛⲟⲛ; Latin: nos</note> <note>common gender</note> | You all <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲑⲱⲧⲉⲛ; Latin: vos</note> | They <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲑⲱⲟⲩ; Latin: illi</note> |

The Copts express the <term>dative</term> <note>the case indicating the recipient of an action, usually translated as "to" or "for"</note> of pronouns with these words: **To me** <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲏⲓ; Latin: mihi</note>, **To you** <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲁⲕ; Latin: tibi</note>, **To him** <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲁϥ; Latin: illi</note>, or for the feminine: **To her** <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲁⲥ</note>.
**Plural:** **To us** <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲁⲛ; Latin: nobis</note>, **To you all** <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲱⲧⲉⲛ; Latin: vobis</note>, **To them** <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲁⲩ; Latin: illis</note>. The remaining <term>cases</term> <note>grammatical categories like possessive or objective</note> of pronouns cannot exist separately from the nouns and verbs to which they are attached, as will be seen.

## CHAPTER II.
### On the Demonstrative and Relative Pronoun.

The <term>Demonstrative</term> <note>words like "this" or "that" used to point to specific things</note> is of two types: the near and the remote.

## Chapter II. On Demonstrative and Relative Pronouns.

| | Near <note>original Latin: Propinquum</note> | Remote <note>original Latin: Remotum</note> | Relative <note>original Latin: Relatiuum</note> |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Singular:** (masc: | ⲫⲁⲓ This. | ⲫⲏⲉⲧⲉⲙⲙⲁⲩ That. | ⲫⲏ Who/Which. |
| (fem: | ⲑⲁⲓ This. | ⲉⲧⲉⲙⲙⲁⲩ That. | ⲑⲏ Who/Which. |
| | | ⲑⲏⲉⲧⲉⲙⲙⲁⲩ That. | |
| | | ⲉⲧⲁⲩ That. | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Plural:** | ⲛⲏ These. | ⲛⲏⲉⲧⲉⲙⲙⲁⲩ Those. | ⲛⲏ Who/Which. <note>common gender</note> |

Note: The relative pronouns ⲫⲏ, ⲑⲏ, and ⲛⲏ also admit the form ⲉⲧⲁⲩ, such as ⲫⲏⲉⲧⲁⲩ or ⲑⲏⲉⲧⲁⲩ (who, which). Sometimes they are used even when ⲫⲏ or ⲑⲏ is omitted. For example, "this man who begat" <note>original Latin: hic vir qui genuit</note> is written ⲡⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓⲫⲏⲉⲧⲁⲩ ⲁϥϫⲫⲟϥ; with ⲫⲏ omitted, it is said ⲡⲓⲣⲱⲙⲓⲉⲧⲁⲩⲁϥϫⲫⲟϥ, which means the same thing. Likewise, "this woman who gave birth to him" <note>original Latin: hæc mulier quæ genuit</note> is written ϯⲥϩⲓⲙⲓⲑⲏⲉⲧⲁⲩ ⲁⲥⲙⲓⲥⲓⲙⲙⲟϥ; it is rendered similarly as ϯⲥϩⲓⲙⲓⲉⲧⲁⲩⲁⲥⲙⲓⲥⲓⲙⲙⲟϥ. However, we shall treat the remaining relative and interrogative pronouns more extensively in the section on adverbs.

# PART IV.

### *On affixes and prefixes and their Logic among the Copts.*

<term>Affixes</term> <note>meaning "attached things"</note> are what we call inseparable pronouns that are joined to the end of nouns; they indicate a possessive meaning. In their placement, the <term>Coptitæ</term> <note>the Copts, the Christian people of Egypt</note> differ from other Eastern languages; for they sometimes place them at the end, and sometimes at the beginning. It will also be evident from what follows that they are even placed in the middle of words. To indicate every kind of possessive meaning, they primarily use eight letters, specifically as many as the diverse— <note>the text cuts off at the catchword "diuer-", likely "diverse persons" or "diverse forms" to be continued on the next page</note>

<summary>This page defines Coptic demonstrative and relative pronouns, illustrating how they are used to identify people and things. It also introduces the concept of affixes—pronouns that attach directly to words—marking a distinction between Coptic and other Near Eastern languages.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 302 regarding the Coptic language's grammatical structure. <header>Part IV. On affixes among the Copts.</header>

The possession of a thing can be considered in various ways. And they are the following, about which I will also speak more extensively elsewhere.

->**ⲁ. ⲓ. ⲕ. ⲛ. ⲧⲉⲛ. ⲉ. ⲣⲉ. ϥ. ⲥ. ⲧ.**<-

1. **ⲁ**. occurring in a word, it indicates the person speaking of themselves, that is, the 1st person of the singular number: **ⲡⲁⲟⲥ** <note>original Latin: Dominus meus</note> My Lord; **ⲡⲁⲓⲱⲧ** <note>original Latin: Pater meus</note> My Father; **ⲡⲁⲛⲟⲩϯ** <note>original Latin: Deus meus</note> My God. Where note that the initial letter **ⲡ**, the masculine gender article, joined to the letter **ⲁ**, constitutes the possessive word in the first person of the masculine gender: as **ⲡⲓⲣⲱⲙⲉ** [means] "Man," with the affix **ⲡⲁⲣⲱⲙⲉ** [means] "My man."

2. **ⲓ** the letter signifies the same first person singular number, which is placed sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at the end. As in **ⲡⲉⲧⲉϩⲛⲏⲓ** <note>original Latin: voluntas mea</note> My will; **ⲁⲓⲥⲁϫⲓ** <note>original Latin: locutus sum</note> I have spoken; **ⲛⲏⲓ** <note>original Latin: mihi</note> to me.

3. **ⲕ** indicates the second person of the masculine gender. For example: **ⲡⲉⲕⲟⲥ** <note>original Latin: Dominus tuus</note> Thy Lord; **ⲡⲉⲕⲓⲱⲧ** <note>original Latin: Pater tuus</note> Thy Father; **ⲡⲉⲕⲛⲟⲩϯ** <note>original Latin: Deus tuus</note> Thy God; **ⲁⲕⲥⲁϫⲓ** <note>original Latin: locutus es</note> Thou hast spoken; **ⲛⲁⲕ** <note>original Latin: tibi</note> to thee.

4. **ⲛ** signifies the first person of the plural number speaking of themselves. As in **ⲡⲉⲛⲟⲥ** <note>original Latin: Dominus noster</note> Our Lord; **ⲡⲉⲛⲓⲱⲧ** <note>original Latin: Pater noster</note> Our Father; **ⲁⲛⲛⲁϩϯ** <note>original Latin: credimus</note> We believe; **ⲉⲣⲟⲛ** <note>original Latin: à nobis</note> from us.

5. **ⲧⲉⲛ** indicates the 2nd person of the plural number. For example: **ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** <note>original Latin: verba vestra</note> Your words; **ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲛⲟⲥ** <note>original Latin: Dominus vester</note> Your Lord; **ⲁⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** <note>original Latin: locuti estis</note> You [plural] have spoken; **ⲛⲏⲧⲉⲛ** <note>original Latin: vobis</note> to you [plural].

6. **ⲉ** indicates the 2nd person present <note>Refers to the person being addressed, specifically in the feminine singular</note> as in **ⲡⲉⲟⲥ** <note>original Latin: Dominus tuus</note> Thy Lord; **ⲧⲉⲟⲥ** <note>original Latin: Domina tua</note> Thy Lady.

7. **ⲣⲉ** indicates the 2nd person present: as in **ⲁⲣⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** <note>original Latin: locuta es</note> Thou [feminine] hast spoken.

<header>Part V. On the Verb and its particles.</header>

# PART V.

## On the Verb and its particles.

I would have many things to say here regarding the various subdivisions of the verb used by the Copts <note>original: "Coptitis"</note>; but since we have reserved that discussion for our *Treasury* <note>Likely referring to Kircher's more comprehensive work, "Lingua Aegyptiaca Restituta"</note>, we will only show here the method they use in the inflection <note>the process of changing a word's form to express grammatical categories</note> of verbs, which is quite different from our own. This is so that our method, with the thornier details removed, might be made easier and clearer for beginners <note>original: "Tyronibus"</note>. It should be noted, therefore, that the Copts use eight characters, or rather particles—now divided into various signs—as an aid to measure every inflection of both nouns and verbs. These mentioned particles are like certain signs or indicators of gender, number, case, person, moods, tenses, and other circumstances that are commonly considered by grammarians in nouns and verbs. Therefore, if you have knowledge of particles of this kind, it will not be difficult to conjugate <note>to list the different forms of a verb</note> any Coptic verb. The particles are the following:

---

| ⲁ. ⲉⲓ | ⲛ | ⲕ | ⲧⲉ | ⲥ | ⲉⲣ | ⲉⲧ | ⲟⲩ. | ⲉⲣⲧⲉⲛ. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

---

But so that we may proceed with greater clarity, we will subdivide this treatise on the verb into as many parts as there are particles, so that the functions of the individual particles or marks occurring in nouns and verbs may be better understood.

### First Division.

And first indeed, the sign **ⲁ. ⲉⲓ** indicates the person speaking of himself in nouns; that is, it denotes the affix <note>a bound grammatical element, here a prefix</note> of the first [person]...

In verbs of the present tense, it has this sign:

1. ϯⲥⲁϫⲓ I speak.

### Second Division.

The letter **N** signifies the person speaking about himself and about another, that is, the companion person <note>Kircher's term for the first-person plural, "we"</note>; and it has fifteen signs. First, in nouns, it has these three signs: **ⲡⲉⲛ**, **ⲛⲉⲛ**, **ⲧⲉⲛ** <note>These are possessive prefixes meaning "our," varying by the gender and number of the noun they modify</note>.
