# Part V. On the Verb and its particles

| | | | |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| <margin>ⲡⲉⲛ</margin> | 1 | **ⲡⲉⲛⲛⲟⲩϯ** | Our Lord. |
| <margin>ⲡⲉⲛ</margin> | 2 | **ⲡⲉⲛⲛⲟⲩϯ** | masculine, of our Lord. |
| <margin>ⲧⲉⲛ</margin> | 3 | **ⲧⲉⲛⲛⲟⲩϯ** | feminine, of our Lady. |

In verbs of the past tense, indeed, it has these 4 signs.

| | | | |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| <margin>ⲁⲛ</margin> | 1 | **ⲁⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** | We have spoken. |
| <margin>ⲉⲧⲁⲛ</margin> | 2 | **ⲉⲧⲁⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** | (when we have spoken, |
| | | | (or when we were speaking. |
| <margin>ⲛⲁⲛ</margin> | 3 | **ⲛⲁⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** | We had spoken. |
| | | | (Because we spoke or |
| <margin>ϣⲁⲛ</margin> | 4 | **ϣⲁⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** | (that we have spoken. |

In verbs of the future, these eight signs are found.

| | | | |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| <margin>ⲉⲑⲣⲉⲛ</margin> | 1 | **ⲉⲑⲣⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** | That we may speak. |
| <margin>ⲛⲉⲛ</margin> | 2 | **ⲛⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** | We shall speak. |
| <margin>ⲉⲛⲛⲁ</margin> | 3 | **ⲉⲛⲛⲁⲥⲁϫⲓ** | We want to speak. |
| <margin>ⲛⲧⲉⲛ</margin> | 4 | **ⲛⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** | That we may speak. |
| <margin>ⲉⲣⲉⲡⲉⲛ</margin> | 5 | **ⲉⲣⲉⲡⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** | We shall speak. |
| <margin>ⲉⲧⲉⲛ</margin> | 6 | **ⲉⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** | Who [we] shall speak. |
| <margin>ⲧⲉⲛ</margin> | 7 | **ⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** | We shall speak. |
| <margin>ϣⲁⲛ</margin> | 8 | **ϣⲁⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** | Because we shall speak. |

Finally, in verbs of the present tense, it has this sign **ⲧⲉⲛ**, as in **ⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ**: we speak or we are speaking.

### Third Division.

The third letter <term>ⲧ</term> <note>The Coptic letter 'Taw'</note> signifies the third person present without an affix <note>This refers to the grammatical construction of the third person where no additional suffix is attached to the stem</note>; it is for the third person and has 14 signs.

## Part V. On the Verb and its particles.

And first, indeed, in nouns it has 3 signs. <note>These prefixes indicate possession by a third-person masculine subject ("his").</note>
| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| ⲡⲉϥ | 1 | ⲡⲉϥⲟⲥ | His Lord (masculine). |
| ⲛⲉϥ | 2 | ⲛⲉϥⲟⲥ | His Lords (masculine plural). |
| ⲧⲉϥ | 3 | ⲧⲉϥⲟⲥ | His Lady (feminine). |

In verbs of the past tense, it has three signs as follows.
| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| ⲁϥ | 1 | ⲁϥⲥⲁϫⲓ | He has spoken. (specifically, that man) |
| ⲉⲧⲁϥ | 2 | ⲉⲧⲁϥⲥⲁϫⲓ | When he had spoken. |
| ⲛⲁϥ | 3 | ⲛⲁϥⲥⲁϫⲓ | He had spoken or he was speaking. |

In verbs of the future tense, however, it has 7 signs, as follows.
| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| ⲉϥⲉ | 1 | ⲉϥⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ | He shall speak. |
| ⲉϥⲛⲁ | 2 | ⲉϥⲛⲁⲥⲁϫⲓ | He wishes to speak or is about to speak. |
| ⲉⲑⲣⲉϥ | 3 | ⲉⲑⲣⲉϥⲥⲁϫⲓ | So that he may speak. |
| ⲛⲧⲉϥ | 4 | ⲛⲧⲉϥⲥⲁϫⲓ | So that he may speak. |
| ⲙⲁⲣⲉϥ | 5 | ⲙⲁⲣⲉϥⲥⲁϫⲓ | He shall speak. |
| ⲉⲧⲉϥ | 6 | ⲉⲧⲉϥⲥⲁϫⲓ | Who shall speak. |
| ϣⲁϥ | 7 | ϣⲁϥⲥⲁϫⲓ | Because he will speak. |

In verbs of the present tense, it has **ⲉϥ**, as in **ⲉϥⲥⲁϫⲓ**:
he himself is speaking, or he speaks.

->Division 4.<-

The fourth letter <term>ⲕ</term> <note>The Coptic letter 'kappa'</note> indicates the second person masculine present, that is, the affix *your*. It has 14 signs. And first, in nouns, it has 3 signs, as follows. <note>In Coptic, possessive pronouns change based on both the gender of the owner and the gender/number of the object owned.</note>
| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| ⲡⲉⲕ | 1 | ⲡⲉⲕⲟⲥ | Your Lord (masculine object). |
| ⲛⲉⲕ | 2 | ⲛⲉⲕⲟⲥ | Your Lords (plural objects). |
| ⲧⲉⲕ | 3 | ⲧⲉⲕⲟⲥ | Your Lady (feminine object). |

In verbs of the past tense, it <note>the prefix for the second-person masculine singular, "you"</note> has 3 signs.

| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **ⲁⲕ** | 1 | **ⲁⲕⲥⲁϫⲓ** | You were speaking or you have spoken. |
| **ⲉⲧⲁⲕ** | 2 | **ⲉⲧⲁⲕⲥⲁϫⲓ** | When you have spoken. |
| **ⲛⲁⲕ** | 3 | **ⲛⲁⲕⲥⲁϫⲓ** | Since you had spoken or you were speaking. |

In verbs of the future tense, it has 7 signs, as follows.

| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **ⲉⲕⲉ** | 1 | **ⲉⲕⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** | You shall speak. |
| **ⲉⲕⲛⲁ** | 2 | **ⲉⲕⲛⲁⲥⲁϫⲓ** | You would wish to speak. |
| **ⲉⲑⲣⲉⲕ** | 3 | **ⲉⲑⲣⲉⲕⲥⲁϫⲓ** | So that you may speak. |
| **ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲕ** | 4 | **ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲕⲥⲁϫⲓ** | So that you may speak. |
| **ⲙⲁⲣⲉⲕ** | 5 | **ⲙⲁⲣⲉⲕⲥⲁϫⲓ** | You shall speak. |
| **ⲉⲧⲉⲕ** | 6 | **ⲉⲧⲉⲕⲥⲁϫⲓ** | You who speak. |
| **ϣⲁⲕ** | 7 | **ϣⲁⲕⲥⲁϫⲓ** | Because you will speak. |

But in verbs of the present tense, it has only the sign **ⲉⲕ**, as in **ⲉⲕⲥⲁϫⲓ**: you are speaking, or you speak.

## Division 5.

**C** <note>The author uses the character 'C' to represent the Coptic letter Sima (ⲥ)</note> indicates an absent feminine person <note>the third-person feminine singular, "she" or "her"</note>, and it has 14 signs. In nouns, indeed, they are as follows.

| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **ⲡⲉⲥ** | 1 | **ⲡⲉⲥⲟⲥ** | Her Lord <note>masculine singular object owned by her</note>. |
| **ⲛⲉⲥ** | 2 | **ⲛⲉⲥⲟⲥ** | Her Lords <note>plural objects owned by her</note>. |
| **ⲧⲉⲥ** | 3 | **ⲧⲉⲥⲟⲥ** | Her Lady <note>feminine singular object owned by her</note>. |

In verbs of the past tense, it has 3 signs, and they are the following.

| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **ⲁⲥ** | 1 | **ⲁⲥⲥⲁϫⲓ** | She has spoken or she was speaking. |
| **ⲉⲧⲁⲥ** | 2 | **ⲉⲧⲁⲥⲥⲁϫⲓ** | When she has spoken. |
| **ⲛⲁⲥ** | 3 | **ⲛⲁⲥⲥⲁϫⲓ** | She had spoken or she was speaking. |

In verbs of the future tense, it has 7 signs as follows.

### Division 6.

Sixthly, the letters **ⲉⲣ** <note>original: "Ερ"</note> indicate the second-person feminine present <note>that is, "you" addressed to a female</note>, and it has 14 signs. And in nouns, indeed, there are 3:
| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **ⲡⲉ** | 1 | **ⲡⲉⲟⲥⲓ** | Your Lord. |
| <margin>f.</margin> **ⲛⲉ** | 2 | **ⲛⲉⲟⲥ** | Your Lords. |
| **ⲧⲉ** | 3 | **ⲧⲉⲟⲥ** | Your Lady. |

In verbs of the past tense, it similarly has 3 signs.
| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **ⲁⲣⲉ** | 1 | **ⲁⲣⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** | You have spoken. |
| **ⲉⲧⲁⲣⲉ** | 2 | **ⲉⲧⲁⲣⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** | When you have spoken. |
| **ⲛⲁⲣⲉ** | 3 | **ⲛⲁⲣⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** | You were speaking. |

In verbs of the future tense, it has 7 signs as follows.
| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **ⲉⲣⲉ** | 1 | **ⲉⲣⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** | You will speak. |
| **ⲉⲣⲡⲁ** | 2 | **ⲉⲣⲡⲁⲥⲁϫⲓ** | So that you may speak. |
| **ⲉⲩⲣⲉ** | 3 | **ⲉⲩⲣⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** | So that you may speak. |
| **ⲛⲧⲉ** | 4 | **ⲛⲧⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** | So that you may speak. |
| **ⲙⲁⲣⲉ** | 5 | **ⲙⲁⲣⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** | Let you speak. |

| | | | |

| **Ⲉⲧⲉ** | 6 | **ⲉⲧⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** | You who speak. |
| **Ϣⲁⲣⲉ** | 7 | **ϣⲁⲣⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** | You speak. <note>original: "Loqueris." This likely refers to the habitual aspect, "you are accustomed to speaking."</note> |

In verbs of the present tense, it has the sign **Ⲉⲣ**, as in **ⲉⲣⲥⲁϫⲓ**, you speak (feminine).

->Division 7.<-

Seventhly. These letters **Ⲟⲩ** and **Ⲁⲩ** signify plural nouns who are absent <note>meaning the third-person plural, "they" or "their"</note>, or the third-person affix. And in nouns, it first has 3 signs:

| | | | |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Ⲡⲟⲩ** | 1 | **Ⲡⲟⲩⲟⲥ** | Their Lord. |
| **Ⲛⲟⲩ** | 2 | **Ⲛⲟⲩⲟⲥ** | Their Lords. |
| **Ⲧⲟⲩ** | 3 | **Ⲧⲟⲩⲟⲥ** | Their Lady. |

In verbs of the future tense <note>The author writes "future" here, but the following examples and their Latin translations actually describe the past tense.</note>, it has 3 signs as follows:

| | | | |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Ⲁⲩ** | 1 | **Ⲁⲩⲥⲁϫⲓ** | They were speaking or they have spoken. |
| **Ⲉⲧⲁⲩ** | 2 | **Ⲉⲧⲁⲩⲥⲁϫⲓ** | When they have spoken. |
| **Ⲛⲁⲩ** | 3 | **Ⲛⲁⲩⲥⲁϫⲓ** | They had spoken. |

In verbs of the future tense, it has 7 signs:

| | | | |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Ⲉⲩⲉ** | 1 | **Ⲉⲩⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** | They will speak. |
| **Ⲉⲩⲛⲁ** | 2 | **Ⲉⲩⲛⲁⲥⲁϫⲓ** | They wish to speak. |
| **Ⲉϣⲉⲩ** | 3 | **Ⲉϣⲉⲩⲥⲁϫⲓ** | So that they may speak. |
| **Ⲛⲧⲉⲩ** | 4 | **Ⲛⲧⲉⲩⲥⲁϫⲓ** | That they may speak. |
| **Ⲙⲁⲣⲉⲩ** | 5 | **Ⲙⲁⲣⲉⲩⲥⲁϫⲓ** | Let them speak. |
| **Ⲉⲧⲉⲩ** | 6 | **Ⲉⲧⲉⲩⲥⲁϫⲓ** | They who will speak. |
| **Ϣⲁⲩ** | 7 | **Ϣⲁⲩⲥⲁϫⲓ** | They will speak. <note>Like the habitual forms above, this often implies "they usually speak."</note> |

In verbs of the present tense, it has the sign **Ⲉⲩ**, as in **Ⲉⲩⲥⲁϫⲓ**, they speak.

# Part V. On the Verb and its particles.
## Division 8.

**Ⲧⲉⲛ**, finally, indicates the second person plural <note>meaning "you" when addressing a group</note>, and it has 14 signs. In nouns, there are 3.

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲛ | 1 | ⲡⲉⲧⲉⲛⲟⲥ | Your Lord. |
| ⲛⲉⲧⲉⲛ | 2 | ⲛⲉⲧⲉⲛⲟⲥ | Your Lords. |
| ⲧⲉⲧⲉⲛ | 3 | ⲧⲉⲧⲉⲛⲟⲥ | Your Ladies. <note>original Latin: "Dominę vestrę," referring to a feminine plural possession.</note> |

->In the past tense it has just as many signs.<-

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| ⲁⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛ | 1 | ⲁⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ | You [plural] have spoken. |
| ⲉⲧⲁⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛ | 2 | ⲉⲧⲁⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ | When you have spoken. |
| ⲛⲁⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛ | 3 | ⲛⲁⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ | You were speaking. <note>original: "Loquebamini," the imperfect tense.</note> |

->In the future tense it has the following seven signs.<-

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| ⲉⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛ | 1 | ⲉⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ | You will speak. |
| ⲧⲉⲧⲉⲛ | 2 | ⲧⲉⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ | You will wish to speak. |
| ⲉⲑⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛ | 3 | ⲉⲑⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ | That you may speak. |
| ⲛⲧⲉⲧⲉⲛ | 2 <note>This number 2 appears to be a typesetting error in the original, as it follows 3 in the sequence.</note> | ⲛⲧⲉⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ | That you may speak. |
| ⲙⲁⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛ | 4 | ⲙⲁⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ | When you speak. |
| ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲉⲛ | 6 | ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ | You who will speak. |
| ϣⲁⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛ | 7 | ϣⲁⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ | You will speak. <note>This often denotes a habitual action: "you are accustomed to speaking."</note> |

In the present tense, it has this sign **ⲧⲉⲧⲉⲛ**, as in **ⲧⲉⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ**, you speak.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Plural number:** | (1 | ⲁⲛ | ⲛⲁⲛ | ⲉⲛ | ⲉⲛⲉ | We |
| | (2 | ⲁⲣⲉ-ⲧⲉⲛ | ⲛⲁⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛ | ⲉⲧⲉⲧⲉⲛ | ⲉⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛ | You [plural] |
| | (3 | ⲁⲩ | ⲛⲁⲩ | ⲉⲩ | ⲉⲩⲉ | They (masc. & fem.) |

From this table, you will learn the conjugation of any verb more quickly than can be told, as is evident in the following examples. Where, if you prefix the particles contained in this preceding table to the roots of the verbs **ⲥⲁϫⲓ** <note>to speak</note>, **ⲥⲱⲧⲉⲙ** <note>to hear</note>, **ⲧⲱⲃϩ** <note>to pray or ask</note>, **ⲧⲱⲛⲕ** <note>to arise</note>, and others, you will have completed the entire conjugation of the verb. But frequent practice and exercise will make all these things easier.

## Example 2.

### Perfect Past.
<note>In this table, the author uses the root **ⲥⲱⲧⲉⲙ** (sōtem), which means "to hear." He is demonstrating how the prefixes change to indicate who is performing the action.</note>

| Singular: | | Plural: | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. I have heard | I have heard. | 1. We have heard | we have heard. |
| 2. You have heard | [you] heard. | 2. You (plural) have heard | [you] heard. |
| 3. He has heard | [he] heard. | 3. They have heard | they heard. |

---

### Imperfect Past.
<note>The Imperfect tense describes an ongoing or repeated action in the past (e.g., "I was hearing"). Interestingly, the author here swaps the labels for the **ⲁ-** and **ⲛⲁ-** prefixes compared to modern Coptic grammars, reflecting the early stage of Coptic studies in the 17th century.</note>

| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. I was | hearing. | 1. We were | hearing. |
| 2. You were (hearing) | hearing. | 2. You (plural) were (hearing) | hearing. |
| 3. He was | hearing. | 3. They were | hearing. |

---

### Present Participle.
<note>original: "Participium præsens." This conjugation typically represents the "circumstantial" present, used to describe an action happening at the same time as another verb.</note>

| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. I | hear. | 1. We | hear. |
| 2. You (hearing) | hear. | 2. You (plural) (hearing) | hear. |
| 3. He | hears. | 3. They | hear. |

---

### Future.

| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. I shall | hear. | 1. We shall | hear. |
| 2. You will (hearing) | hear. | 2. You (plural) (hearing) | hear. |
| 3. He will | hear. | 3. They will | hear. |

---

Imperative <note>The command form</note>: **Hear!**
You will conjugate other verbs in the same way, such as **ⲧⲱⲛⲕ** <term>to rise</term>, **ⲱⲣⲕ** <term>to swear</term>, [and] **ⲧⲱⲃϩ** <term>to ask or pray</term>.
Therefore, let it suffice to have presented only two [examples] here.

### method of the Easterners.

| **2** | (**ⲁⲕⲥⲁϫⲓ**<br>(**ⲁⲣⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** fem: | You have spoken.<br> | **2** | **ⲁⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** | You (pl.)<br>have spoken. |

<note>In Latin: "Præteritum Imperfectum." This describes an ongoing or habitual action in the past (e.g., "I was speaking").</note>

| | | | | | |
|:---:|:---|:---|:---:|:---|:---|
| **1** | **ⲛⲁⲓⲥⲁϫⲓ** | I was speaking. | **1** | **ⲛⲁⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** | We were speaking. |
| **2** | (**ⲛⲁⲕⲥⲁϫⲓ**<br>(**ⲛⲁⲣⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** fem: | You were speaking. | **2** | **ⲛⲁⲣⲉⲧⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** | You (pl.) were<br>speaking. |

## Imperative.

3 ( **ⲉϥⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** he will speak <note>original: "loquetur"</note>. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **ⲉⲩⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** they will speak <note>original: "loquentur"</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp; ( **ⲉⲥⲉⲥⲁϫⲓ** feminine: <note>she will speak</note>

->Imperative.<-

**ⲁϫⲓ** : Speak (masculine), speak (feminine), speak (plural). It always remains invariable; the plural is recognized only from the context, as was said above. <note>In Coptic, some verbs do not change their form when addressing a man, a woman, or a group.</note>

## On the Imperative.

Note that in verbs, sometimes the tenses occur without the aforementioned signs <note>The "signs" refer to the prefix particles typically used to indicate tense and person.</note>, just as in the Imperative as follows:
**ⲧⲱⲛⲕ** &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; rise (masculine)
**ⲧⲱⲛⲏⲓ** &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; rise (feminine)
**ⲧⲱⲛⲑⲏⲛ** &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; rise (common/plural)
**ⲙⲁϣⲉⲛⲁⲕ** &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; go away (masculine)
**ⲙⲁϣⲉⲛⲉ** &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; go away (feminine)
**ⲙⲁϣⲉⲛⲱⲧⲉⲛ** &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; go away (common/plural)
**ⲁⲙⲟⲩ** come (masculine) **ⲁⲙⲏ** come (feminine) **ⲁⲙⲱⲓⲛⲓ** come (plural).

Sometimes they are without signs, and that is true of every active verb. <note>Active verbs in Coptic often use their simple root form for the imperative command without needing a prefix.</note>

### On the negative particle to be used in the Imperative.

The Copts, when indicating a prohibition, place the negative particle **ⲙⲡⲉⲣ** <note>pronounced 'mper'</note> before the Imperative, meaning "do not" or "not." For example: **ⲙⲡⲉⲣⲟⲩⲱⲙ** <note>original Arabic: لا تاكل ("la ta'kul")</note> do not eat. **ⲙⲡⲉⲣⲁⲣⲓ** do not do.

Sometimes this negative particle is used not only in the Imperative but also in the remaining moods and persons, such as in the future or subjunctive, by prefixing this particle **ⲙⲡ** <note>pronounced 'mp'</note>, meaning "not." For example:

| | | | |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **ⲙⲡⲓⲟⲩⲱⲙ** | let me not eat. | **ⲙⲡⲓⲥⲱ** | let me not drink. |
| **ⲙⲡⲉⲕⲟⲩⲱⲙ** | let you not eat. | **ⲙⲡⲉⲕⲥⲱ** | let you not drink. |
| **ⲙⲡⲟⲩⲟⲩⲱⲙ** | let them not eat. | **ⲙⲡⲟⲩⲥⲱ** | let them not drink. |

There are also among the Egyptians <note>The author refers to the Coptic-speaking people as Egyptians</note> as many different negative particles as there are different letters that change the meaning of things in number and person. We have indeed numbered eight of these above, to each of which corresponds the following individual negative particles:

| | | | | | |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **ⲙⲡⲓ** | not I. | **ⲙⲡⲉⲛ** | not we. | | |
| **ⲙⲡⲉϥ** | not he. | **ⲙⲡⲉⲕ** | not you (masc.). | **ⲙⲡⲉⲥ** | not she. |
| **ⲙⲡⲉ** | not you (fem.). | **ⲙⲡⲟⲩ** | not they. | **ⲙⲡⲉⲧⲉⲛ** | not you (plural). |

->Example.<-

**ⲙⲡⲓⲥⲁϫⲓ** I shall not speak. **ⲙⲡⲉϥⲥⲁϫⲓ** he shall not speak <note>The Latin original has "f." after "non loquatur," but the Coptic prefix ⲙⲡⲉϥ refers to a masculine "he."</note>.

| | | |
| :--- | :---: | :--- |
| **ⲙ̀ⲡⲉⲛⲥⲁϫⲓ** | | let us speak. |
| **ⲙ̀ⲡⲉⲩⲥⲁϫⲓ** | | let them speak. |

From these examples, you will observe that no change occurs in the verb itself, <term>ⲥⲁϫⲓ</term> <note>original Coptic: "saji", meaning "to speak"</note>, but rather in the negative particle which carries the meaning. If you understand this principle well, you will have overcome a great part of the difficulty of Coptic Grammar. But more will be said on these matters in their proper place.

## CHAPTER VI.

->On the nature of affixes<-

Just as among all the Eastern peoples <note>original Latin: "Orientales," referring to the Semitic and Afro-Asiatic speaking worlds</note>—such as the Hebrews, Syrians, Chaldeans, Arabs, and Ethiopians—possessive pronouns are not indicated by separate words as they are in our languages, but by certain particles which are called "affixes" because they are usually attached to the end of nouns and verbs; so too the Egyptians <note>The author uses "Egyptians" to refer to the Coptic people</note> use certain particles which, when joined to nouns and verbs, function as affixes. These are twofold, as follows:

| | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **ⲉⲣⲟⲓ** | 1st person sing. common | **ⲙ̀ⲙⲟⲓ** | me. |
| **ⲉⲣⲟⲛ** | 1st person plur. common | **ⲙ̀ⲙⲟⲛ** | us. |
| **ⲉⲣⲟϥ** | 3rd person sing. masc. | **ⲙ̀ⲙⲟϥ** | him. |
| **ⲉⲣⲟⲕ** | 2nd person sing. masc. | **ⲙ̀ⲙⲟⲕ** | you. |
| **ⲉⲣⲟⲥ** | 3rd person sing. fem. | **ⲙ̀ⲙⲟⲥ** | her. |

## Example using the verb <term>ⲁⲛⲁⲩ</term> <note>original Coptic: "anau", meaning "to see"</note>

### Past perfect

**ⲁⲛⲁⲩⲉⲣⲟⲓ** — He saw me.
**ⲉⲧⲁⲩⲛⲁⲩⲉⲣⲟⲕ** — that is: When he saw you;
**ⲛⲁⲩⲛⲁⲩⲉⲣⲟ** — He saw you (feminine).

### Future

**ⲉϥⲉⲛⲁⲩⲉⲣⲱⲟⲩ** — He will see them.
**ⲉϥⲛⲁⲛⲁⲩⲉⲣⲱⲧⲉⲛ** — I will see you <note>In the original Latin text, "Videbo vos" (I will see you), though the Coptic prefix ⲉϥⲛⲁ- usually indicates "He will". The author often adapts Coptic to fit Latin grammatical models.</note>.
**ⲉⲑⲣⲉϥⲛⲁⲩⲉⲣⲟ** — So that he might see you.
**ⲛⲧⲉϥⲛⲁⲩⲉⲣⲓ** — So that he might see me.
**ⲙⲁⲣⲉϥⲛⲁⲩⲉⲣⲱⲟⲩ** — Let him see them.
**ⲉⲧⲉϥⲛⲁⲩⲉⲣⲟϥ** — He who saw him.
**ϣⲁϥⲛⲁⲩⲉⲣⲟⲛ** — When he saw us.

In the present tense, **ⲉϥⲛⲁⲩⲉⲣⲟϥ**, he sees him. In the Imperative: **ⲁⲛⲁⲩⲉⲣⲟϥ** see him; **ⲁⲛⲁⲩⲉⲣⲟⲓ** see me; and so on for the rest. Finally, so that nothing might be missing from our Coptic Grammar, it seemed fitting to add here a certain summary table in which everything said so far might be contained as if in a brief overview <note>original Latin: "anacephaleosi", a term derived from Greek meaning a summary or recapitulation of main points</note>. Its use is as follows: having chosen a verb root, look for the tense, person, gender, and number on the right side, and the possessives, moods, and tenses at the bottom of the table; the intersecting cell will then provide the affix that should be added to the root.

# SECTION VI.
## Concerning Adverbs and other particles used by the Copts
### CHAPTER I.

The Copts count a great many types of such <term>particles</term><note>A general term used by historical grammarians to describe small, unchangeable words like adverbs, prepositions, and conjunctions.</note> according to their various meanings and constructions. These indeed are the most common:

### Chapter III. On the Ecclesiastical Reckoning of the Copts.

And indeed, the Copts borrowed those previous numbers from the Greeks. Furthermore, besides those, they have other numbers which are native to them, as follows:

->The native method of counting used by the Copts.<-

| 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **One.** <note>original: "Ⲟⲩⲁⲓ" (*Ouai*)</note> | **Two.** <note>original: "ⲥⲛⲁⲩ" (*Snau*)</note> | **Three.** <note>original: "ϣⲟⲙⲧ" (*Shomt*)</note> | **Four.** <note>original: "ϥⲧⲱⲟⲩ" (*Ftoou*)</note> | **Five.** <note>original: "ⲧⲓⲟⲩ" (*Tiou*)</note> | **Six.** <note>original: "ⲥⲟⲟⲩ" (*Soou*)</note> | **Seven.** <note>original: "ϣⲁϣϥ" (*Shashf*)</note> |

### CHAPTER III.

### On the Ecclesiastical Reckoning of the Copts.

The Copts have twelve months and one intercalary <term>intercalary: a period inserted into the calendar to keep it aligned with the solar year</term> month, concerning which we read the following in their own books.

> Twelve months; and the thirteenth is Nisi, which is the addition made every 4 years at the beginning of the year. <note>original: "Ⲛⲓⲁⲃⲟⲧ ⲙⲉⲧⲥⲛⲁⲩ..."</note>

That is, there are twelve Coptic months, the thirteenth of which is *Nisi*, which arises from the addition of five days made every 4 years, etc. They call the remaining 5 intercalary days either the *added days* <note>original: "ἐπαγομένας" (*epagomenas*)</note> or also *Nisi*, because of the hieroglyphic symbol of a serpent biting its own tail <note>the Ouroboros, a symbol of cyclical time and eternity</note> which represents them; as the *Onomasticum* <note>a Greek lexicon or book of names</note> shows.

Their year is three hundred and sixty-five days. <note>original Arabic: سنتهم ثلثماية وخمسة وستين يوما</note>
The fifth day of Nisi is the leap day every four years at the start of the year. <note>original Arabic: خامس النسى يوم الكبيس فى كل اربع سنين بدو السنة</note>
Nowruz <note>original Arabic: النوروز. This refers to the Coptic New Year, known as Nayrouz, derived from the Persian word for "New Day".</note>

## Chapter III. On the Ecclesiastical Reckoning of the Copts.

-> Nowruz, and it is a Persian word. <note>original Arabic: النوروز وهي لفظه فارسيه</note> <-

This year of theirs contains 365 days. Five days, called *Nisi* <term>Nisi</term> <note>From the Coptic word for "intercalary days" or "epagomenal days"</note>, are intercalated every four years at the beginning of the year *Nowruz* [Nuruz], etc. We have seen what *Nisi* is above in Chapter 4 of the *Prodromus* <note>Kircher refers to his own work, *Prodromus Coptus sive Aegyptiacus* (1636)</note>; and we also hinted at it a little earlier. We shall explain what *Nowruz* means shortly thereafter.

It should be known, therefore, that just as the Egyptians called their year **Canicular** <term>Canicular year</term> <note>A year measured by the "heliacal rising" of the star Sirius (the Dog Star or Canicula), which signaled the annual flooding of the Nile</note>, which consisted of four simple years and an additional day. So too the **Ancient Persians** called their four-year period **Nowruz** <note>original: نوروز (*Neuruz*)</note>. For to them, *Nowruz* is the beginning of spring, which literally means **new day**, as if you were to say "new day" in Greek <term>new day</term> <note>original Greek: νέαν ἡμέραν (*nean hēmeran*)</note>. For just as the Egyptians observed the rising of the Dog Star, because of which the flooding of the Nile occurred, so too the Persians to this very day establish the beginnings of spring not only as the era and title of their civil calendar, but they also celebrate it with feasts and processions, as Fernão Lopes <note>Fernandus Lopez, likely the Portuguese historian Fernão Lopes de Castanheda, who wrote on the history of India and the East</note> testifies in his *History of India*, book 1, chapter 46. Today, however, that name *Nowruz* is not only on the lips of the Persians, but also among other nations, to the extent that the **Turks** call the solar year *Nowruz* <note>original: نوروز</note>. And when they wish to indicate someone's age, they say he has as many *Nowruz* as the years he has lived. The Persians, therefore, called their year *Nowruz*, just as the Egyptians called theirs *Canicular*. Moreover, just as the Egyptians used the term **Year of God** <term>Year of God</term> <note>original Greek: ἐνιαυτὸν Θεοῦ (*eniauton Theou*)</note>, so they [the Persians] used **Saal chodai** <note>original Persian: سال خودای (*Saal chodai*)</note>, the **Year of God** or **Year of the Sun**. From this, astrologers call the period of solar years in the **releasers** <term>releasers</term> <note>original Greek: ἀφετικοῖς (*aphetikois*), referring to the *apheta*, a planet or point in a birth chart used by ancient astrologers to calculate the length of a person's life</note> of human life *Salchodai*. But the Egyptians differed from the Persians and Chaldeans in this: that they [the Egyptians] let the "reins loose" for their month of **Thoth** <note>The first month of the Egyptian and Coptic calendars</note> and did not intercalate. For as many days as there were from the new moon of the first *Thoth*, so many four-year periods and years...

...canicular [years], or the **Year of God** <term>Year of God</term> <note>original Greek: ἐνιαυτὸς Θεοῦ (*eniautos Theou*)</note>, they numbered. The Chaldeans and Persians, however, because each day of a single month was named after Heroes or Kings, called the first four-year period by the name of the first day; the second, by the name of the second; about all of which, God willing, [I will write] more fully in the third part of our *Egyptian Oedipus* <note>Kircher's massive four-volume work on Egyptology and Coptic studies</note>. Now let us return to the Coptic reckoning.

Therefore, as I said in the *Prodromus* <note>Kircher's *Prodromus Coptus sive Aegyptiacus* (1636)</note>, the Copts establish the era of their years from the first year of Diocletian. The beginning of his reign, according to the calculations of Theon <note>Theon of Alexandria, a 4th-century mathematician and astronomer</note>, fell in the Augustan year of the victory at Actium <note>Refers to the era starting from the Battle of Actium (31 BC), which the Romans used to mark the beginning of their rule in Egypt</note>, an epoch which the Egyptians have used for their timing until now. At which time the year of the Jewish period was 4997, and the Solar Cycle of Actium was 5. And although the consummation of the Coptic Martyrdom occurred in the 19th year of Diocletian, the Era of the Martyrs by no means begins from this year, but from the first [year]—as we said. The reason for this seems to be that not only the Egyptians, but also the Romans used this Era of Diocletian. Therefore, so as not to deviate from the Roman and Egyptian era, they retained the same customary era, which they also called [the era] of the Martyrs. The Romans, however, under Constantine, changed the aforementioned Era of Diocletian into the epoch of Indictions <term>Indictions</term> <note>A 15-year cycle used in the Roman Empire for tax assessments and dating</note>. Furthermore, they divide the years passed since this Era of Martyrs into certain cycles, which they themselves, along with the Latins, call the **Solar Cycle** <term>Solar Cycle</term> <note>original Greek/Coptic transliteration: πικυκλος ὴ τρη (*pikyklos hē trē*)</note>, that is, the Cycle of the Sun. With the help of these [cycles], they seek the Paschal month [Easter], as we shall teach in its proper place. Moreover, the Coptic Christians have their own feasts or solemnities to be celebrated throughout the course of the whole year, and they are as follows:

# CONCEPT
->or<-
## GROUND-PLAN OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

**F**urthermore, nothing now remains but to present here a certain idea or <term>ground-plan</term> <note>original Greek: ἰχνογραφία (*ichnographia*), referring to an architectural floor plan or a detailed outline</note> of the works that are to follow. It was for the sake of these future works that we sent forth this *Forerunner* <note>original: *Prodromus*</note> to the <term>Republic of Letters</term> <note>The international community of scholars and intellectuals in the 17th century</note>, as we promised in the Preface to the Reader. Once this is provided, I hope that all who have ever read anything on a similar subject, or have noted anything worthy of observation elsewhere—in whatever language or field of study—will not refuse to share those findings with me, moved by their concern for the advancement of the common good.

And first, if it should so please God the Best and Greatest, the *Egyptian Oedipus* <note>Kircher's monumental work (published 1652–1654) where he attempted to solve the "riddle" of hieroglyphs, naming it after Oedipus, the mythical solver of the Sphinx's riddle</note> will follow closely after the *Forerunner* and the *Arabic-Coptic-Latin Treasury* (the organization, usefulness, and excellence of which we discussed above in Chapter 8, pages 196 and 197). We have designated this three-part work as follows: the first part, the *Egyptian Temple*; the second, the *Hieroglyphic Gymnasium*; and finally the third, the *Hieroglyphic Theater*. Behold, then, the plan of this three-part work in the following sections.

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS
## PART I.
### THE EGYPTIAN TEMPLE.

->Divided into six <term>treatises</term> <note>original: *syntagmata*, referring to organized collections of knowledge</note> as if into certain inner sanctuaries, in which the origins of idolatry and the sources of the first superstition are revealed and demonstrated from their very foundations.<-

->In which<-

In this section, through a parallel comparison, it is taught that the deities of all the Greeks and ancient Romans originated from nowhere else but Egypt <note>Kircher was a leading proponent of "diffusionism," the theory that all ancient wisdom and religion originated in Egypt and spread to other cultures</note>.

Idea or Ground-plan of the Egyptian Oedipus:

# *Class I. Hieroglyphic Grammar.*

->In which<-

The various literature and philology of the Egyptians, its proximity to the Hebrew <term>Cabala</term> <note>A Jewish mystical tradition that Kircher believed originated in Egypt</note>, and finally the first instruction in hieroglyphics through a parallel comparison with the Cabala, is investigated.

# *II. Class of Hieroglyphic Physics.*

->In which<-

The hidden characteristics of nature, and the *signatures* <note>The "Doctrine of Signatures" was the belief that plants and minerals carried physical signs—like shape or color—that revealed their medicinal or spiritual use</note> (as they are called) of individual natural things, from which the Ancients were accustomed to form hieroglyphic characters, are explained.

# *III. Class of Hieroglyphic Medicine.*

->In which<-

The medical art and the various Egyptian methods of healing, represented hieroglyphically, are set forth; it contains within it the science of <term>Simples</term> <note>Medicines made from a single natural ingredient, such as a specific herb or mineral</note>; it reveals the hidden and unknown science of stones, plants, trees, fruits, seeds, spices, vegetables, animals, and the virtues concealed within them.

# *IV. Class of Hieroglyphic Mathematics*

Contains within itself Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, Astronomy, Architecture, Statics, and <term>Thaumaturgy</term> <note>The art of creating mechanical wonders or "miracles" through engineering</note>, or concerning the prodigious machines of the ancient Egyptians, the mysteries of which, lying hidden beneath hieroglyphics, are brought to light.

# *V. Class of Hieroglyphic Magic.*

Discusses both types of Magic <note>Referring to "Natural Magic" (science) and "Superstitious Magic" (sorcery)</note> of the ancient Egyptians; which contains within it Chemistry <note>original: *Chymia*, referring here to Alchemy</note>, the [fabrication] of Astrological Images...

*Scene V.* It unearths the mummies and explains their history, origin, and mystical wrappings.

*Scene VI.* It presents the statues of Isis <note>original: "Isiacas"</note> and other monuments marked with hieroglyphs.

In all of these matters, with the help of the grace of the Divine Power, we shall assert nothing that is not established from all types of ancient monuments and the hidden archives of the Latins, Greeks, Hebrews, Syrians, Arabs, Chaldeans, Ethiopians, Samaritans, Persians, Indians, and others, and confirmed by legitimate authority.

And this is the Plan <note>original: "Idea"</note> of our *Oedipus*, the first part of which we have now completed in all its parts <note>original: "omnibus numeris," a Latin idiom meaning "perfectly" or "in every respect"</note>; our industry is currently exerting itself entirely on the refinement of the second and third parts. May God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Deus O. M." - *Deus Optimus Maximus*</note>, grant that it may serve solely for the glory of His name, the benefit of Holy Mother Church, and the good of the entire Republic of Letters <term>Reipublica literaria</term> <note>The international community of scholars and intellectuals</note>.

<summary>Kircher lists the physical Egyptian artifacts he will interpret in the final section of his work, including obelisks, the Bembine Tablet, and mummies, while asserting that his research is based on a vast array of linguistic and historical archives.</summary>

<keywords>Obelisks, Bembine Tablet, Canopic jars, Sphinxes, Mummies, Statues of Isis, Republic of Letters, Archives, Chronology of work</keywords>

<meta>This page is the beginning of the "Ad Lectorem" (To the Reader) preface. It follows the errata and Coptic prayer translations from the previous page. The catchword "am-" suggests the next page begins with a word like "amplecter" (to embrace).</meta>

## TO THE READER.

*SINCE I have the intention of restoring the whole of Egyptian antiquity, the sheer difficulty of the subject matter suggested that I should begin this entire project with the very thing that serves as the key to all of antiquity: the ancient native language of the Egyptians, which we call Coptic or Pharaonic.* *The usefulness of this language is immense across every field, art, and science. It contributes not only to the study of secular literature but also to sacred texts—in short, to unearthing all ancient learning and erudition. Although this <note>original: "Prodromus," referring to this book, the *Prodromus Coptus* (1636), which acted as a "precursor" to his later works</note> Precursor demonstrates this extensively in various sections, I hope that my* *Egyptian Oedipus <note>Athanasius Kircher’s future masterpiece, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* (1652–1654), in which he attempted to decode Egyptian hieroglyphs</note> will demonstrate this even more clearly and abundantly through the diverse knowledge it uncovers by this means. I also hope it will inspire lovers of more profound literature not only to value this language—newly introduced to Europe—but also to devote all their study and effort to learning it.* *To make this easier to achieve, I have chosen to attach the <term>lessons</term> <note>original: "institutiones," referring to the grammar and foundational rules of the language</note> of said language to the end of this work. This is so that the reader may practice them in the meantime, making themselves more capable and better prepared to understand what is to come.* *I have also included an <term>Outline</term> <note>original: "Idea," a conceptual map or summary</note> of the entire Egyptian Oedipus for no other reason than to show the reader how much the <term>Republic of Letters</term> <note>the international community of scholars and intellectuals</note> stands to gain from the restoration of both these literatures.* *My friends certainly know this; I have shown them glimpses of these hidden secrets, as if through narrow cracks. Deeply moved by the novelty of these findings, and having no other way to express it, they have vied with one another to praise this work in the introductory poems found at the start of this Precursor.* *However, I did not wish to place an obstacle to divine favor by accepting the praises of men, nor did I want to greedily [seek out] such small comforts...*

<summary>Athanasius Kircher introduces his work on the Coptic language, framing it as the essential "key" to unlocking the mysteries of ancient Egypt and his future research on hieroglyphs.</summary>
<keywords>Athanasius Kircher, Coptic language, Egyptian antiquity, Oedipus Aegyptiacus, Republic of Letters, Pharaonic language, translation, philology</keywords>

--- Page 350 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface "Ad Lectorem" (To the Reader). The text begins mid-sentence, concluding a thought from the previous page where Kircher explains his caution in publishing such a grand work. The catchword "am-" from the previous page matches the start of "ambisse" (to have sought/canvassed for) here.</meta>

# To the Reader.

*...lest I should seem to have **sought glory**, or even to have celebrated triumphs before the victory, I declined their praised kindness with the modesty that was fitting; except for the commendations of those who were to be not so much givers of praise, as witnesses and approvers of various matters.* *For since this present book is a <note>original: "Prodromus," meaning a precursor or preliminary publication</note> Precursor to the project of my **Oedipus**—a work entirely new, rare, difficult, and of a subject matter that many consider unbelievable—and since many things, drawn from the hidden and unseen monuments of the East, remain entirely hidden from Europeans who lack knowledge of these languages, many might perhaps doubt my reliability in such new matters, or suspect some kind of imposture or trickery.* *So that I might proceed in a matter of such great weight with greater transparency, faith, and sincerity, and at the same time show that—by divine grace—I am not ignorant of the languages I will bring forward throughout my works to confirm my statements, I wished to admit as witnesses those very Greeks, Hebrews, Syrians, Chaldeans, Arabs, Armenians, Ethiopians, Abyssinians, Samaritans, and others to whom my <term>literary equipment</term> <note>original: "literaria supellex," referring to his collection of books, manuscripts, and research tools</note> is known, and who have examined and reviewed all my work; and who, with advice and help at all times, strive to the best of their ability to promote the work I have undertaken by sharing things from their own resources.* *And these, kind reader, are the things I wanted to advise you of first; if you find anything worthy of praise in them, I would wish you to attribute it not to me, but to God, the giver of all good things, who alone makes the tongues of infants eloquent. Farewell.*

<summary>Kircher explains that he has invited experts in various Eastern languages to witness and verify his research to avoid accusations of fraud or inaccuracy in his "Egyptian Oedipus" project. He concludes the preface by humbly attributing his linguistic abilities and scholarly successes to divine grace.</summary>
<keywords>Athanasius Kircher, Oedipus Aegyptiacus, linguistic expertise, Eastern languages, scholarly verification, divine grace, Coptic studies, 17th-century scholarship</keywords>

# MUTIO VITELLESCHI
## OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS
### SUPERIOR GENERAL.

**S**ince three members of the same Society <note>The Society of Jesus, commonly known as the Jesuits</note>, to whom the task was entrusted, have reviewed the **Coptic** or **Egyptian Precursor** <note>original: "Prodromus," meaning a preliminary work or introductory treatise</note> of Father Athanasius Kircher of our Society, and have approved that it may be published; we grant permission for it to be printed, provided it so pleases the Most Reverend Lord <term>Vicegerent</term> <note>The deputy of the Cardinal Vicar of Rome, responsible for ecclesiastical administration</note> and the Most Reverend Father <term>Master of the Sacred Palace</term> <note>The Pope’s primary theologian, responsible for censoring and authorizing books in Rome</note>. In witness of this, we have issued these letters, signed by our own hand and secured with our seal. At Rome, 23rd of April, 1635.

*Mutio Vitelleschi.*

**B**y order of the Most Reverend Father Brother Nicolaus Riccardi, <term>Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace</term> <note>The Pope’s chief theologian and primary book censor</note>; I have duly and in order examined the book of Father Athanasius Kircher of the Society of Jesus, titled *The Coptic Precursor*, or *Egyptian* <note>original: "Prodromus Coptus, seu AEgyptiacus"</note>. In it, I have not only found nothing contrary to the Catholic Religion and good morals, but on the contrary, many arguments ingeniously brought to light from the hidden secrets of sacred antiquity and the mystical inner chambers of the Egyptians. These arguments—owing both to his genuine knowledge of many languages and to his profound scholarship in foreign matters drawn directly from the original sources—provide strength and support for the orthodox truth and dismantle errors and heresies. It is a worthy beginning, by which all his other works may be judged. This study, born of a fortunate labor of discovery and genius, will flourish for a long time, "passing the torch" (as the saying goes) <note>original: "lampada... tradens," an ancient metaphor for the transmission of knowledge from one person to another, like a relay race</note> to all learning, both Sacred and secular. Such is my judgment. At Rome, from the <term>Professed House</term> <note>The central residence and headquarters of the Jesuit Order in Rome</note>, June 15, Year 1636.

# Isaac of Shidra, Maronite Archbishop of Tripoli in Syria, to the Very Reverend Father, his most beloved, Athanasius Kircher of the Society of Jesus

## A Syriac Rhythm in the Jacobite Chant
<note>Isaac Shidrawi (c. 1590–1663) was a Maronite bishop who assisted Kircher with Syriac and Arabic. "Jacobite" refers to the West Syriac liturgical tradition, which the Maronites share, though they are in communion with Rome.</note>

A hidden narrative and an exceeding wonder: Praise be to Him who chose Abraham from his father's house and delivered Isaac from a certain thicket <note>original: "sekitha," referring to the ram caught in the thicket during the Binding of Isaac in Genesis 22</note>, making His power wonderful to Abraham. An upright hymn <note>original: "qumita," a type of Syriac liturgical poem performed while standing</note>.

-> A discourse of newness and wonder. <-

**A** — The Chosen Christ came, a certain thing to Abraham ——— <note>This is an alphabetical acrostic poem; each line begins with a successive letter of the Syriac alphabet.</note>
**B** — In the house of transition <note>or "traveling"</note> with Isaac the son, to Abraham ———
**G** — Revealed was the command and the flash of the sword to Abraham ———
**D** — Who stood in the tent, hearing the [voice] <note>Syriac: "ddaya," potentially referring to the "breasts" or "nurture" of the promise</note> of Abraham ———
**H** — They became kings as one from heaven, as is right and proper.
**W** — And He set for them many and wonderful things to say.
**Z** — A hidden kind, that builds the sanctuary as they require.
**H** — They rejoiced immediately, that God was for His son as they prepared.
**T** — Blessed is he who comes in his soul, for knowledge departs.
**Y** — They know and they shall know, and for the goal of all the kingdoms.
**K** — Love restrained [the hand], and the Lord was likened [to him], and the voice of song.
**L** — To God a portion of light, and God in the house of the altar.
**M** — God is understood by all nations in His glory in everything.
**N** — It goes out in a breath toward existence, that it might not depart.
**S** — He supports us all, and He is in the waters of life.
**E** — With salvation may there be a possession in Your fear.
**P** — He saved mankind for salvation by means of Christ.

<summary>A dedicatory poem in Syriac by the Maronite Archbishop Isaac Shidrawi to Athanasius Kircher, utilizing an alphabetical acrostic to reflect on the Sacrifice of Isaac as a prototype of Christ's salvation.</summary>

## The same author's literal translation.

**M**y Father, Venerable Doctor, most famous Athanasius: you who in your teachings strive to imitate the Great Doctor Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373), the defender of orthodoxy against Arianism</note>; you imitate those chosen and splendid stars, Basil <note>St. Basil the Great (330–379), one of the Three Holy Hierarchs</note>, and in your knowledge you imitate the Sun of the Church, Gregory <note>St. Gregory of Nazianzus (329–389), known as "The Theologian" for his eloquence</note>. Our Lord has given you a sublime intellect in the abundance of His mercies, and the understanding of all philosophers. He has clothed you with the armor of all the sciences, as befits those who are sent to accomplish noble tasks. His power has assisted you in learning the voices <note>original: "voces," meaning languages or tongues</note> just as His chosen ones do. May your acquaintances, your friends, your masters, and the Doctors grant great happiness to your understanding soul, because you manifest the wisdom of all the Eastern peoples and the knowledge of many languages beyond all others. You teach among the Doctors; you have quickly learned the idioms of various speeches and revealed them with ease. The book which you have printed, and the others which you intend to print, you illuminate most easily with the explanation and commentary of words; you subtly ponder and penetrate the languages you encounter. You labor much, yet you present your findings briefly and elegantly. Receive this hymnody, which I send to you from my heart, distinguished Doctor, and which I offer to you in *Syriac*. Glory be to the Good One who has directed you and led you truly; thanksgiving be to the Spirit, who has brought you to the goal without stumbling.

<summary>A poetic and prose tribute by Isaac Shidrawi praising Athanasius Kircher as a modern successor to the Church Fathers and a master of Oriental languages. The text highlights Kircher's intellectual labors and his ability to "penetrate" difficult ancient tongues.</summary>
<keywords>Athanasius Kircher, Isaac Shidrawi, Syriac, Church Fathers, St. Basil, St. Gregory, Orientalism, linguistics, Maronite, panegyric</keywords>

# THE COPTIC FORERUNNER
## SYLLABUS OF CHAPTERS
## AND HEADINGS.

### Preface to the Forerunner

*The reason for writing; the difficulty of treating ancient matters; the antiquity of the Coptic language; the encouragement of eminent men toward this kind of writing. The Coptic-Arabic Treasury <note>This refers to Kircher's lexicon, the "Lingua Aegyptiaca Restituta," which he viewed as a "treasury" or "thesaurus."</note> is presented first as the base and foundation of the Hieroglyphic work.*

---

### Chapter I.
### On the etymology of the word Coptos.

*Coptos is derived not from Egypt, nor "Chibt," but from the City of Coptos <note>A city in Upper Egypt, modern Qift.</note>. What the Greek term "Gyptios," the Coptic* <note>original: "Γυπτιος"</note> *the Arabic* **Qibti** <note>original: "قبطي"</note>, *and likewise* **Misr** *and* **Misri** <note>original: "مصر" & "مصرى"</note> *or Mestra <note>A reference to Mizraim, the biblical name for Egypt.</note> actually signify. The difference between* **Koptos** *and* **Cophthos**. *What is the Ethiopic word "Gobzo"? A description of the City of Coptos. Called "Cana" by Ramusio and "Elitron" by Hegesippus; its fame and fertility.*

---

### Chapter II.
### On the institutions of the Coptites.

*The Coptites were most devoted to the worship of Idols before Christ. After Christ, they were the first to be imbued with the Christian religion; a city near the Thebaid <note>The region surrounding the ancient city of Thebes in Egypt.</note>. The Coptites rescued the ancient Egyptian language from destruction. Coptic books in the Vatican Library. Religious zeal flourishes among the Coptites. A huge number of Martyrs. What is the Era of Martyrs? <term>Era of Martyrs<gloss>Also known as the Diocletian Era, the calendar used by the Coptic Church which begins in 284 AD, marking the start of the Roman Emperor Diocletian's reign and his subsequent persecution of Christians.</gloss></term> The rites of the Coptites in administering the sacraments. The nature of the Coptic Liturgy. The Coptic and Ethiopic Church were once one under the Bishop <note>original: "Antistite," referring to the Pope of Alexandria.</note> of Alexandria. How much such ancient liturgies can benefit the conversion of Heretics.*

---

### Chapter III.
### On the Colonies of the Coptic-Ethiopic Church established in other parts of the world.

*Coptites, Egyptians, and Ethiopians once used the Syriac language in sacred rites. From Egypt, Syria, and Ethiopia into India for the propagation of the faith*

## Chapter IV.

## On the aforementioned colonies led into India, China, Japan, and Tartary.

*What and where Cathay <note>original: "Catbaia"</note> actually is. Who and where that great Prester John <note>original: "Presbyter Ioannes," a legendary Christian patriarch and king popular in European chronicles</note> is located. Concerning Griffins and Pygmies, and whether these are properly considered human. ## Chapter V.

*The Coptic or ancient Egyptian language was once related to Greek. An examination of the Coptic or Egyptian name. **Zaphenath-Paneah** <note>original: "Thaphnat fanech"; the name given to Joseph by Pharaoh in Genesis 41:45</note> or **Psontomphanich**. On account of the miracles performed, the Egyptians call Moses **Psontomphanicli**, which means "revealer of secrets"; Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic, Chaldean, Samaritan, Greek, Armenian, and Coptic texts regarding this name are discussed. The Coptic language was not related to Hebrew nor to other Oriental languages, except for Greek. A passage from Benjamin <note>A reference to the 12th-century traveler Benjamin of Tudela</note> is explained regarding the Egyptian language. The name "Moses" as an Egyptian name and its meaning. A comparison of the Coptic language with other Oriental languages. The months of the Ancient Egyptians, and the names of the stars and other things, such as herbs, animals, and Gods, which the Coptic language still retains the same as the ancient Egyptian. **Asima** is not an Egyptian name, but Samaritan.*

## Chapter VI.

## On the Coptic Name of God Ⲫϯ Ptah <note>original: "Phtha"</note>.

*It is a mystical name. The logic of mystical names. Various monograms. The mysteries of Armenian letters. The mysteries of the Coptic name **Ⲫϯ** <note>The standard Coptic word for God</note> are explained. Who Ptah, the ancient God of the Egyptians, was. His generation from **Hemepht** <note>Kircher's interpretation of a creator deity, often linked to the concept of the "World Soul"</note>. Ptah as a symbol of the world; the name uni-*

...traversing the whole world. *Various characters of Phtha or Thoth <note>original: "Phta seu Tauti," referring to Egyptian deities Kircher associates with early writing</note> are still found among the Hieroglyphs, which is why the staff of Saint Anthony is marked with the sign of the Tau.* What was the shape of the staff of Moses? ### Chapter VII.

*The Greek language first flowed from the Egyptian language. Notable points regarding the sign for the Greek number six <note>The stigma</note>, which is still used among the Copts as the sixth letter of the alphabet. ### Chapter VIII.

->**On the Utility of the Coptic Language.**<-

*The utility of the Coptic language is greatest not only for refuting heresies, but also for cultivating other branches of learning. A treasury of Coptic books in the Vatican Library, and a catalog of them. The excellence of the Coptic-Arabic treasury <note>Referring to bilingual lexicons and grammars</note>. The alphabet of the Agarenes <note>A term for Arabs/Muslims, as descendants of Hagar</note> or Africans. A true, certain, and faithful interpretation of a wonderful and very ancient inscription carved into a certain rock on Mount Horeb <note>Mount Sinai</note>, explained by no one before this: in which many hidden things are drawn out from the antiquities of the Hebrews.*

### Chapter IX.

*It is shown through various examples that Coptic words were inserted into hieroglyphic letters. Various monograms are clarified: to which is finally added a specimen of hieroglyphic interpretation; in which many things concerning the symbolic disciplines of the ancient Egyptians, mentioned by no one (as far as I know) before this, are brought forth with new daring and effort. To all of which is attached at the end a particular treatise on the elements of the Coptic language, which it pleased me to designate as the "First Fruits of the Coptic or Egyptian Language"; together with the "Plan of the Oedipus" <note>Kircher's preview for his massive future work, "Oedipus Aegyptiacus," which attempted to fully decode hieroglyphics</note>.*
